questions.explanation: After 'So' + adjective at the start, the verb comes before the subject: So loud was the noise.

wrongReasons.loudly: After 'So' we need an adjective (loud) because it describes the noun 'noise'. 'Loudly' is an adverb.
wrongReasons.louder: 'louder' is a comparative form. Here we need the basic adjective after 'So'.

questions.text: So ___ was the noise that we could not hear each other.

questions.explanation: 'Were it not for' + noun means 'if it hadn't been for'.

wrongReasons.by: The fixed phrase is 'Were it not for'.
wrongReasons.of: The fixed phrase is 'Were it not for'.

questions.text: Were it not ___ your help, I would have failed.

questions.explanation: In cleft sentences with 'All … did', use 'was' + base form: All she did was smile.

wrongReasons.is: The action happened in the past (did), so the verb is 'was'.
wrongReasons.to: 'to' alone leaves the sentence without a verb; the pattern is 'All I did was + base form'.

questions.text: All I did ___ ask a simple question, and she walked out.

questions.explanation: After 'recommend/suggest/insist that', use the base form (or 'should' + base form): She suggested that he stop.

wrongReasons.stops: After 'recommended that' formal English uses the base form, with no -s.
wrongReasons.stopped: The subjunctive is always the base form; 'stopped' is not used here.
wrongReasons.to stop: 'recommend that' is followed by a clause with the base form, not by 'to'.

questions.text: The doctor recommended that he ___ smoking at once.

questions.explanation: After 'Not only' at the start of a sentence, put the auxiliary before the subject: Not only did he apologise, but he also paid.

wrongReasons.does: The race happened in the past (broke), so use 'did'.
wrongReasons.had: 'had' would need a past participle (had she won), but the verb here is 'win'.

questions.text: Not only ___ she win the race, but she also broke the national record.

questions.explanation: After negative phrases such as 'Under no circumstances' at the start, use inversion: Under no circumstances should you open this door.

wrongReasons.is: 'visitors' is plural, so the verb must be 'are'.
wrongReasons.be: 'be' is the base form; the inverted verb must be a full form: are visitors allowed.

questions.text: Under no circumstances ___ visitors allowed to feed the animals.

questions.explanation: Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle, … would have + past participle: Had she asked, I would have helped.

wrongReasons.will: This is about an unreal past situation, so 'will have' is not possible in the result clause.
wrongReasons.had: 'had have' is wrong; the result clause needs 'would/could/might' + have + past participle.

questions.text: Had I known about the traffic, I ___ have left much earlier.

questions.explanation: A law or rule 'comes into force' (or 'comes into effect') when it starts to apply.

wrongReasons.power: 'come into power' is used for governments or leaders, not laws.
wrongReasons.action: 'come into action' is not used for laws; we say 'come into force'.

questions.text: The new regulations will come into ___ next January.

questions.explanation: 'Up in the air' means not yet decided: Our holiday plans are still up in the air.

wrongReasons.sky: The idiom is fixed: 'up in the air', never 'up in the sky'.
wrongReasons.clouds: 'Have your head in the clouds' means to be a dreamer; this idiom uses 'air'.

questions.text: I can't give you a final answer yet; the whole plan is still up in the ___.

questions.explanation: Use 'is said/believed/thought + to have + past participle' for an earlier action: He is thought to have escaped.

wrongReasons.to: 'to left' is impossible; for a past action use the perfect infinitive 'to have left'.
wrongReasons.having: After 'is believed' use a to-infinitive, not the -ing form.
wrongReasons.to had: After 'to' always use the base form 'have', not 'had'.

questions.text: The suspect is believed ___ left the country last week.

questions.explanation: 'Without which' means 'if this had not existed or happened': She had a map, without which she would have got lost.

wrongReasons.despite: 'despite which' would mean the research did not help, but the sentence says it was necessary.
wrongReasons.with: 'with which' cannot express the idea 'if it had not invested'.

questions.text: The firm invested heavily in research, ___ which it would never have overtaken its rivals.

questions.explanation: A 'stalemate', 'deadlock' or 'impasse' is a situation in which neither side can make progress.

wrongReasons.stop: 'reach a stop' is not natural here; use 'stalemate', 'deadlock' or 'impasse'.
wrongReasons.block: 'reach a block' is not idiomatic; the word is 'deadlock'.

questions.text: The negotiations reached a ___ when neither side would make any concessions.

questions.explanation: 'Hammer out' (or 'thrash out') means to reach an agreement after long discussion: They hammered out a deal.

wrongReasons.knock: 'knock out' means to make someone unconscious or eliminate them from a competition.
wrongReasons.make: 'make out' means to see or understand something with difficulty, not to reach an agreement.

questions.text: The negotiators will have to ___ out a compromise that both sides can accept.

questions.explanation: Use 'It was … that' to emphasise one part of a past sentence: It was Tom who called.

wrongReasons.is: The event happened last night (kept), so the cleft uses 'was'.
wrongReasons.were: In 'It was … that' sentences, 'It' always takes a singular verb.

questions.text: It ___ the noise, not the heat, that kept me awake last night.

questions.explanation: After 'Rarely' at the start, put the auxiliary before the subject: Rarely have I seen such a view.

wrongReasons.have: The subject is 'such a talented young player' (singular), so use 'has'.
wrongReasons.did: 'did' would need the base form 'emerge', but the verb here is 'emerged'.

questions.text: Rarely ___ such a talented young player emerged from the local league.

questions.explanation: 'If need be' is a fixed phrase with the old subjunctive 'be'; it means 'if necessary'.

wrongReasons.is: 'If need be' is a fixed expression that keeps the subjunctive form 'be'.
wrongReasons.arises: We can say 'if the need arises', but the short fixed phrase is 'if need be'.

questions.text: If need ___, we can always postpone the launch by a week.

questions.explanation: 'But for' + noun means 'if it had not been for': But for your help, I would have failed.

wrongReasons.without: 'but without' is not a phrase; 'but for' already means 'without'.
wrongReasons.of: The fixed expression is 'but for', not 'but of'.

questions.text: But ___ the goalkeeper, we would have lost by five goals.

questions.explanation: A 'vested interest' is a personal reason, often financial, for wanting something to happen.

wrongReasons.invested: The fixed phrase is 'vested interest', not 'invested interest'.
wrongReasons.vast: 'vast interest' would mean a lot of curiosity; it does not suggest personal gain.

questions.text: He has a ___ interest in the outcome, since his company stands to gain millions.

questions.explanation: A 'compelling' or 'cogent' argument is so clear and logical that it convinces people.

wrongReasons.compulsive: 'compulsive' describes behaviour that is hard to stop, not an argument that convinces.
wrongReasons.convinced: 'convinced' describes a person who is sure; an argument is 'convincing'.

questions.text: Her argument was so ___ that even her fiercest critics had to accept it.

questions.explanation: The formal pattern is 'be requested (not) to + base form': Guests are requested not to use the pool after 10 p.m.

wrongReasons.to not: In formal notices 'not' comes before 'to': requested not to smoke.
wrongReasons.don't: After 'requested' use a to-infinitive: 'not to smoke'.

questions.text: Passengers are kindly requested ___ smoke anywhere on board.

questions.explanation: In a 'What' cleft, the clause 'What really annoyed the committee' is singular, so we use 'was': What surprised me was the price.

wrongReasons.were: The subject is the whole 'What...' clause, which is singular, so 'were' is wrong even before a plural-sounding idea.
wrongReasons.is: The sentence is about a past event (annoyed), so the present 'is' does not match the tense.

questions.text: What really annoyed the committee ___ the lack of any written evidence.

questions.explanation: We say 'deal a blow to something' when something is badly damaged: The news dealt a blow to our hopes.

wrongReasons.hit: 'deal a hit' is not a natural collocation; the verb 'deal' goes with 'blow'.
wrongReasons.damage: 'damage' is uncountable and is not used with 'deal a'; we 'cause damage'.

questions.text: The scandal dealt a severe ___ to the senator's chances of re-election.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional uses 'if + past perfect' for a past condition and 'would + base verb' for a present result: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

wrongReasons.has: The condition refers to a past moment (last year) that did not happen, so we need the past perfect 'had approved'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'would have' is not used in the if-clause; use 'had' + past participle.

questions.text: If the committee ___ approved the funding last year, the bridge would be finished by now.

questions.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' means to stop arguing and become friends again: The two brothers finally buried the hatchet.

wrongReasons.sword: We 'lay down our swords', but the idiom for ending a quarrel is 'bury the hatchet'.

questions.text: After weeks of tense negotiations, the union finally agreed to bury the ___.

questions.explanation: After a negative adverbial like 'Never before' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Never before had I seen such beauty.

wrongReasons.did: 'witnessed' is a past participle here, so the auxiliary must be 'had' or 'has', not 'did'.
wrongReasons.was: 'was witnessed' would be passive and does not fit with 'the city' as the one who saw.

questions.text: Never before ___ the city witnessed such a massive demonstration.

questions.explanation: 'However' (or 'though') placed mid-sentence between commas introduces a contrast: The room was nice; the view, however, was awful.

wrongReasons.therefore: 'therefore' shows a result, but the second idea contrasts with the first.
wrongReasons.moreover: 'moreover' adds a similar point, but here the idea is opposite.

questions.text: The hotel was comfortable; the food, ___, left a great deal to be desired.

questions.explanation: The pattern 'It was only when... that...' emphasises a time clause: It was only when I left that I understood.

wrongReasons.when: 'when' is already used in the focus part; the cleft needs 'that' to link to the main clause.
wrongReasons.which: 'which' cannot introduce the second part of an 'It was... that' cleft about a time.

questions.text: It was only when the lights went out ___ we realised how isolated the cabin was.

questions.explanation: 'Reach an amicable settlement/agreement' means to end a dispute in a friendly way: They reached an amicable settlement out of court.

wrongReasons.solution: 'amicable' describes relations between people; we say 'amicable settlement', not 'amicable solution'.
wrongReasons.decision: A decision is made by one side; 'amicable' collocates with 'settlement' or 'agreement'.

questions.text: The two companies finally reached an amicable ___ after months of legal wrangling.

questions.explanation: 'Should + subject + verb' is a formal way to say 'If': Should you have any questions, call me.

wrongReasons.would: 'Would' cannot replace 'if' at the start of a conditional.
wrongReasons.had: 'Had you need' is ungrammatical; 'Had' is followed by a past participle.

questions.text: ___ you need any further information, please do not hesitate to contact us.

questions.explanation: 'The tip of the iceberg' is a small, visible part of a much bigger problem: These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.

wrongReasons.mountain: The idiom is 'the tip of the iceberg', not 'mountain'.
wrongReasons.icecube: The idiom refers to an 'iceberg', whose larger part is hidden underwater.

questions.text: The new tax is just the tip of the ___; far bigger cuts are planned.

questions.explanation: 'Little did + subject + know' means the person had no idea: Little did she know that he was lying.

wrongReasons.had: With the base verb 'know', the auxiliary must be 'did', not 'had'.
wrongReasons.were: 'were know' is ungrammatical; the inverted auxiliary is 'did'.

questions.text: Little ___ the passengers know that the captain had never flown this route before.

questions.explanation: 'Despite' / 'Notwithstanding' + noun introduces a contrast: Despite the rain, we went out.

wrongReasons.although: 'Although' must be followed by a clause (subject + verb), not a noun phrase.
wrongReasons.despite of: We say 'despite' or 'in spite of', never 'despite of'.

questions.text: ___ the overwhelming evidence, the jury failed to reach a verdict.

questions.explanation: A 'What' cleft puts the focus at the end: What I need is a holiday.

wrongReasons.that: 'That' cannot start a clause meaning 'the thing which'; we need 'What'.
wrongReasons.which: 'Which' needs a noun before it; to mean 'the thing that' we use 'What'.

questions.text: ___ I find hard to accept is that nobody bothered to tell us in advance.

questions.explanation: 'Shed (new) light on something' means to help explain it: The letters shed light on his early life.

wrongReasons.lights: The idiom uses uncountable 'light', not the plural.
wrongReasons.information: We 'give information', but the fixed phrase with 'shed' is 'shed light on'.

questions.text: The documentary sheds new ___ on the causes of the financial crisis.

questions.explanation: 'On condition that' means 'only if': You can go on condition that you are home by ten.

wrongReasons.conditions: The fixed phrase uses the singular 'condition'.
wrongReasons.the condition: The fixed phrase is 'on condition that', without 'the'.

questions.text: I'll lend you the car on ___ that you bring it back with a full tank.

questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret by mistake: Who let the cat out of the bag?

wrongReasons.box: The idiom is 'out of the bag', not 'box'.
wrongReasons.sack: The fixed form of the idiom uses 'bag'.

questions.text: I didn't mean to let the cat out of the ___ about the surprise party.

questions.explanation: 'Only after + clause' at the start causes inversion in the main clause: Only after he left did I notice the gift.

wrongReasons.had: The verb 'realise' is in the base form, so we need 'did', not 'had'.
wrongReasons.the scientists did: After 'Only after...', the auxiliary must come before the subject, not after it.

questions.text: Only after the results were published ___ the scientists realise their mistake.

questions.explanation: 'Consequently', 'therefore' and 'as a result' introduce a result: The road was closed; consequently, we were late.

wrongReasons.nevertheless: 'nevertheless' introduces a contrast, but the cancellation is a result of the closure.
wrongReasons.whereas: 'whereas' compares two facts within one sentence and cannot follow a semicolon like this.

questions.text: The museum will be closed for renovation; ___, all school visits have been cancelled.

questions.explanation: In 'It is... that' clefts the focused noun is followed by 'that' (or 'which' for things): It is the noise that bothers me.

wrongReasons.what: 'what' already contains its own noun ('the thing that'), so it cannot follow 'the cost'.
wrongReasons.who: 'who' is for people; 'the cost' is a thing.

questions.text: It is not the cost ___ worries me but the time it will take.

questions.explanation: 'Bring someone to tears' means to make them cry: The ending brought me to tears.

wrongReasons.crying: The fixed phrase uses the noun 'tears', not the -ing form 'crying'.
wrongReasons.tear: The phrase always uses the plural 'tears'.

questions.text: Her performance was so moving that it brought the audience to ___.

questions.explanation: 'If it hadn't been for + noun' means 'without' in the past: If it hadn't been for you, I would have failed.

wrongReasons.wasn't: The result is in the past (would have drowned), so we need 'hadn't been', not 'wasn't'.
wrongReasons.wouldn't have been: 'would' is not used in the if-clause; use the past perfect.

questions.text: If it ___ for the lifeguard's quick reaction, the boy would have drowned.

questions.explanation: 'Catch someone off guard' means to surprise them when they are not prepared: The question caught her off guard.

wrongReasons.balance: 'off balance' is about physical stability; for surprise we say 'off guard'.
wrongReasons.hand: 'off hand' (offhand) means casual or without thought, not surprised.

questions.text: The interviewer's question caught the minister off ___, and he struggled to reply.

questions.explanation: 'Hardly had + subject + past participle + when' means one thing happened immediately after another: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

wrongReasons.did: 'started' here is a past participle after the perfect, so the auxiliary must be 'had'.
wrongReasons.was: 'was started' changes the meaning to passive; the pattern is 'Hardly had... when'.

questions.text: Hardly ___ the meeting started when the fire alarm went off.

questions.explanation: 'Even though / although' + clause introduces a surprising contrast: He kept running even though he was injured.

wrongReasons.despite: 'despite' cannot be followed directly by a clause with a subject and verb.
wrongReasons.even if: 'even if' is for imaginary or uncertain situations; here not being paid is a fact.

questions.text: She agreed to chair the meeting, ___ she was not paid for the extra work.

questions.explanation: 'The reason (why)... was that...' is a common cleft-like structure: The reason I came was that I was worried.

wrongReasons.is because: 'The reason... is because' repeats the idea of cause and is avoided in careful C2 English; use 'was/is that'.
wrongReasons.were: 'The reason' is singular, so the verb must be singular.

questions.text: The reason she resigned ___ that she felt her ideas were constantly ignored.

questions.explanation: 'Come under (heavy) fire/criticism' means to be strongly criticised: The coach came under fire after the defeat.

wrongReasons.blame: We 'take the blame' or 'get the blame'; 'come under blame' is not a collocation.
wrongReasons.pressures: 'pressure' is uncountable in this phrase; 'come under heavy pressures' is wrong.

questions.text: The government has come under heavy ___ for its handling of the floods.

questions.explanation: 'Supposing' introduces an imaginary situation and is followed by a past form for an unlikely event: Supposing you lost your job, what would you do?

wrongReasons.is: With 'would' in the main clause, the condition needs a past form ('were/was'), not 'is'.
wrongReasons.will be: 'will' is not used after 'Supposing' in this kind of conditional.

questions.text: Supposing the flight ___ cancelled, what would you do?

questions.explanation: 'A false economy' is something that seems to save money but costs more in the end: Cheap shoes are a false economy.

wrongReasons.saving: The fixed expression is 'a false economy', not 'false saving'.
wrongReasons.bargain: 'false bargain' is not an idiom; we say 'a false economy'.

questions.text: Buying a cheap printer turned out to be a false ___, as the ink cost a fortune.

questions.explanation: 'No sooner... than' links two actions that happened one right after the other: No sooner had we arrived than it rained.

wrongReasons.when: 'when' is used with 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely'; 'No sooner' needs 'than'.
wrongReasons.then: 'then' is an adverb of time; the comparative 'sooner' needs 'than'.

questions.text: No sooner had the band left the stage ___ the crowd began chanting for an encore.

questions.explanation: 'Whereas / while' compares two contrasting facts: My sister loves maths, whereas I hate it.

wrongReasons.however: 'however' cannot join two clauses with only a comma; it needs a semicolon or full stop.
wrongReasons.because: 'because' gives a reason, but the clauses here show a contrast.

questions.text: Some critics praised the film's daring structure, ___ others found it confusing.

questions.explanation: 'All + subject + verb + was (to) + infinitive' means 'the only thing': All I want is some peace.

wrongReasons.were: 'All' here means 'the only thing', which is singular, so we need 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: The verb 'wanted' is past, so the cleft verb should be past too.

questions.text: All the minister wanted ___ to avoid a public argument before the election.

questions.explanation: 'In imminent danger of + -ing/noun' means something bad will happen very soon: The bridge is in imminent danger of falling.

wrongReasons.risk: We say 'at risk of', not 'in imminent risk of'.
wrongReasons.threat: We say 'under threat of', not 'in imminent threat of'.

questions.text: Scientists warn that the coral reef is in imminent ___ of collapse.

questions.explanation: 'Had it not been for' is the inverted form of 'If it hadn't been for': Had it not been for the rain, we would have won.

wrongReasons.if: 'If' needs 'it had not been', not 'it not been'; the inverted form uses 'Had'.
wrongReasons.were: 'Were it not for' refers to the present; the past result 'would have caught' needs 'Had'.

questions.text: ___ it not been for the delay, we would have caught the last ferry.

questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means slightly ill: I'm feeling a bit under the weather.

wrongReasons.rain: The idiom is 'under the weather', not 'under the rain'.
wrongReasons.clouds: 'under a cloud' means under suspicion, not ill.

questions.text: She's been under the ___ all week, so she won't be coming to the party.

questions.explanation: 'Not until + time' at the start of a sentence causes inversion in the main clause: Not until midnight did they arrive.

wrongReasons.did: The verb is passive (allowed), so the auxiliary is 'were', not 'did'.
wrongReasons.was: The subject 'women' is plural, so we need 'were'.

questions.text: Not until the 1920s ___ women allowed to join the club as full members.

questions.explanation: 'Thereby / thus + -ing' shows a result of the previous action: He resigned, thereby avoiding a scandal.

wrongReasons.whereby: 'whereby' means 'by which' and introduces a relative clause with a subject and verb.
wrongReasons.therefore: 'therefore' is not normally followed directly by an -ing clause like this.

questions.text: The treaty was signed in 1648, ___ ending thirty years of war.

questions.explanation: In 'It was + person + who/that + verb' the focus is on the person: It was Anna who called.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' is for things, but 'the junior researcher' is a person.
wrongReasons.whom: 'whom' is an object form; here the person is the subject of 'noticed'.

questions.text: It was the junior researcher, not the professor, ___ first noticed the anomaly in the data.

questions.explanation: 'Protest one's innocence' means to insist that you did not do something wrong: She protested her innocence throughout the trial.

wrongReasons.innocent: After 'his' we need the noun 'innocence', not the adjective 'innocent'.
wrongReasons.guilt: Nobody 'protests their guilt'; the idea is denying guilt by insisting on innocence.

questions.text: Despite the evidence, the defendant continued to protest his ___.

questions.explanation: 'As long as' / 'so long as' means 'only if': You can stay as long as you're quiet.

wrongReasons.how: 'how long as' is not a conjunction; the phrase is 'as long as'.
wrongReasons.for: 'for long as' is wrong; the phrase is 'as long as'.

questions.text: You can borrow my notes, ___ long as you return them by Friday.

questions.explanation: 'Give someone the cold shoulder' means to ignore them deliberately: After the argument, she gave him the cold shoulder.

wrongReasons.frozen: The idiom is 'cold shoulder', not 'frozen shoulder' (which is a medical condition).
wrongReasons.cool: The fixed form of the idiom is 'cold shoulder'.

questions.text: Ever since their argument, Mark has been giving his sister the ___ shoulder.

questions.explanation: 'On no account' means 'under no circumstances' and is followed by inversion: On no account should you open this door.

wrongReasons.will: 'will' describes a prediction; for a strict rule we need 'should' or 'must'.
wrongReasons.does: 'does be' is ungrammatical; we need a modal before 'be'.

questions.text: On no account ___ the patient be left alone during the night.

questions.explanation: 'In case' means 'as a precaution because something might happen': Take a coat in case it gets cold.

wrongReasons.if: 'if' would make the backup happen only after the theft, which is too late.
wrongReasons.so that: 'so that' introduces a purpose, but nobody wants the laptop to be stolen.

questions.text: You should back up your files regularly ___ your laptop is stolen.

questions.explanation: Clefts can begin with 'Where' to focus on a place or point: Where we differ is in our methods.

wrongReasons.was: The rest of the sentence (falls) is in the present, so 'was' breaks the tense.
wrongReasons.are: The 'Where...' clause is treated as singular, so 'are' is wrong.

questions.text: Where the plan falls down ___ in its assumption that interest rates will stay low.

questions.explanation: We 'establish/build/develop a rapport with someone': He built a strong rapport with his students.

wrongReasons.made: 'make a rapport' is not a natural collocation.

questions.text: The new manager quickly ___ a good rapport with her team.

questions.explanation: In advice with 'If I were you', formal English uses 'were' for all persons: If I were you, I'd call her.

wrongReasons.am: The situation is imaginary, so the present 'am' is wrong.
wrongReasons.had been: The advice is about now, not the past, so 'had been' is wrong.

questions.text: If I ___ you, I would get a second opinion before agreeing to surgery.

questions.explanation: 'Don't put all your eggs in one basket' means don't risk everything on one plan: Spread your investments; don't put all your eggs in one basket.

wrongReasons.bag: The fixed form of the proverb is 'in one basket'.

questions.text: Don't put all your eggs in one ___; invest in several different funds.

questions.explanation: 'Seldom' at the start causes inversion: Seldom have I heard such nonsense.

wrongReasons.have: The subject 'a debut novel' is singular, so 'has', not 'have'.
wrongReasons.does: 'received' is a past participle here, so the auxiliary must be 'has' or 'had'.

questions.text: Seldom ___ a debut novel received such universal praise.

questions.explanation: 'Moreover / furthermore / what's more' add a further, often stronger point: The flat is small; moreover, it's noisy.

wrongReasons.however: 'however' introduces a contrast, but the second point adds another problem.
wrongReasons.otherwise: 'otherwise' means 'if not', which makes no sense here.

questions.text: The proposal is too expensive; ___, it would take years to implement.

questions.explanation: With 'What + subject + did', we use 'was (to) + base verb': What she did was leave early.

wrongReasons.were: A 'What... did' clause is singular, so 'were' does not agree.
wrongReasons.was playing: After 'What... did was', we use the bare infinitive (play), not a continuous form.

questions.text: What the orchestra did next ___ play the entire symphony again from memory.

questions.explanation: 'Pose a threat/risk to' means to be a danger to: Pollution poses a threat to wildlife.

wrongReasons.problem: We say 'pose a problem for', and 'problem' is too weak for a danger to whole communities.
wrongReasons.harm: 'harm' is uncountable and does not follow 'pose a serious'; we 'cause harm'.

questions.text: Rising sea levels pose a serious ___ to coastal communities.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if... not': We'll miss the train unless we hurry.

wrongReasons.if: 'if the samples are kept' gives the opposite meaning; the failure happens if they are not kept stable.
wrongReasons.except: 'except' is a preposition and cannot introduce a full clause in this way.

questions.text: The experiment will fail ___ the samples are kept at a constant temperature.

questions.explanation: 'At the eleventh hour' means at the last possible moment: The strike was called off at the eleventh hour.

wrongReasons.minute: We say 'at the last minute' or 'at the eleventh hour', not 'the eleventh minute'.
wrongReasons.moment: 'the eleventh moment' is not an idiom.

questions.text: The deal fell through at the eleventh ___ when the buyer withdrew.

questions.explanation: 'So + adverb + auxiliary + subject + that' is an emphatic inversion: So quickly did he run that nobody caught him.

wrongReasons.brilliant: The word describes how he performed (a verb), so we need an adverb, not an adjective.
wrongReasons.much: 'So much did he perform' talks about quantity, not quality, and sounds unnatural.

questions.text: So ___ did the actor perform that the audience gave him a ten-minute ovation.

questions.explanation: Adverb + 'speaking' (strictly, broadly, roughly speaking) comments on how a statement should be understood: Strictly speaking, tomatoes are fruit.

wrongReasons.strict: Before 'speaking' we need an adverb, not the adjective 'strict'.
wrongReasons.honest: We say 'honestly speaking' with an adverb, and the idea of an estimate needs 'roughly' or 'strictly'.

questions.text: The figures are, ___ speaking, only an estimate.

questions.explanation: 'It wasn't until + time/event + that + clause' stresses when something finally happened: It wasn't until midnight that he arrived.

wrongReasons.when: The fixed pattern is 'It wasn't until... that', not 'when'.
wrongReasons.then: 'then' is an adverb and cannot link the two parts of the cleft.

questions.text: It wasn't until the final chapter ___ the narrator's true identity became clear.

questions.explanation: Strong adjectives like 'scathing', 'blistering' and 'withering' collocate with 'attack' and 'criticism': The report was a scathing attack on the management.

wrongReasons.hard: 'hard attack' is not a natural collocation; we say 'scathing' or 'fierce attack'.
wrongReasons.heavy: 'heavy' collocates with 'criticism' or 'fire', not 'a heavy attack' in speech.

questions.text: The opposition leader made a ___ attack on the government's tax policy.

questions.explanation: After an inverted third conditional, the result clause uses 'would/could/might have + past participle': Had I known, I would have helped.

wrongReasons.will: The past unreal result needs 'would/could/might have', not 'will have'.
wrongReasons.can: 'can have been saved' does not express an unreal past result.

questions.text: Had the warning been issued earlier, thousands of lives ___ have been saved.

questions.explanation: 'The last straw' is the final problem that makes a situation unbearable: His rudeness was the last straw.

wrongReasons.drop: We say 'the last drop' in some languages, but the English idiom is 'the last straw'.
wrongReasons.stone: 'the last stone' is not an English idiom.

questions.text: Having to rewrite the whole report was the last ___ — I handed in my notice the next day.

questions.explanation: 'Such + be + noun + that' is an emphatic inversion meaning 'the demand was so great': Such was his anger that he left.

wrongReasons.were: 'the demand' is singular, so the verb must be 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: The story is in the past (crashed), so we need 'was'.

questions.text: Such ___ the demand for tickets that the website crashed within minutes.

questions.explanation: 'Few, if any' means 'very few or possibly none': Few, if any, students passed.

wrongReasons.or: 'Few or any' is not an English expression; we say 'few, if any'.
wrongReasons.even: 'Few, even any' is not a fixed phrase.

questions.text: Few, ___ any, of the original buildings survived the earthquake.

questions.explanation: An 'It was + place + that' cleft focuses on the place: It was in Rome that they married.

wrongReasons.there: 'There was' introduces existence; the cleft for emphasis uses 'It was'.
wrongReasons.this: 'This' points to something already mentioned; the cleft structure needs the empty subject 'It'.

questions.text: ___ was in Lisbon that the two writers met for the first and only time.

questions.explanation: We say 'fall badly/seriously/far/well behind schedule': The work fell badly behind schedule.

wrongReasons.heavy: An adjective cannot modify the verb phrase 'fall behind'; we need an adverb.

questions.text: The project fell ___ behind schedule after the main contractor went bankrupt.

questions.explanation: The second conditional uses 'if + past simple' for an unreal present: If she were taller, she would play basketball.

wrongReasons.is: The situation is unreal (he is not careful), so we need a past form.
wrongReasons.would be: 'would' does not go in the if-clause.

questions.text: If he ___ more careful with money, he wouldn't always be borrowing from his friends.

questions.explanation: 'Neck and neck' means exactly level in a competition: The runners were neck and neck until the end.

wrongReasons.head: The idiom is 'neck and neck', not 'neck and head'.
wrongReasons.shoulder: 'shoulder to shoulder' means side by side in support, not level in a race.

questions.text: The two candidates are neck and ___ in the latest opinion polls.

questions.explanation: 'Only by + -ing' at the start causes inversion: Only by practising daily can you improve.

wrongReasons.we can: After 'Only by...', the auxiliary goes before the subject: 'can we'.
wrongReasons.do: 'do we hope' changes the meaning; the modal 'can' expresses possibility here.

questions.text: Only by working together ___ we hope to solve this crisis.

questions.explanation: 'Although / even though' + clause introduces a contrast: They continued, although they were exhausted.

wrongReasons.in spite of: 'in spite of' must be followed by a noun or -ing form, not a clause.
wrongReasons.since: 'since' gives a reason, but slim chances are a reason to stop, not to continue.

questions.text: The rescue team kept searching through the night, ___ their chances of finding survivors were slim.

questions.explanation: 'The thing that/which...' is followed by 'was/is' and the focus: The thing that matters is your health.

wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun like 'the thing'; use 'that' or 'which'.
wrongReasons.who: 'who' is used for people, not for 'the thing'.

questions.text: The thing ___ impressed the judges most was the originality of her design.

questions.explanation: 'It is common knowledge that...' means that everyone knows it: It is common knowledge that he is leaving.

wrongReasons.sense: 'common sense' means practical good judgement, not information everybody knows.
wrongReasons.information: We do not say 'common information'; the fixed phrase is 'common knowledge'.

questions.text: It is common ___ that the two ministers do not get on.

questions.explanation: 'Were + subject + to-infinitive' is a formal, inverted conditional for an unlikely future: Were you to need help, I would come.

wrongReasons.should: 'Should' is followed by a base verb (Should you change), not by 'to change'.
wrongReasons.if: 'If you to change' is ungrammatical; the inverted form needs 'Were'.

questions.text: ___ you to change your mind, the offer would still be open until Friday.

questions.explanation: 'Blow your own trumpet' (US: horn) means to boast about yourself: She never blows her own trumpet.

wrongReasons.whistle: 'blow the whistle' means to report wrongdoing, not to boast.
wrongReasons.drum: We 'bang the drum' for a cause; the idiom for boasting is 'blow your own trumpet'.

questions.text: He's always blowing his own ___, telling everyone how successful he is.

questions.explanation: 'Scarcely had + subject + past participle + when' shows one event followed immediately by another: Scarcely had we left when it snowed.

wrongReasons.did: 'opened' is a past participle after the perfect, so 'had' is needed.
wrongReasons.has: The narrative is in the past, so 'has' is the wrong tense.

questions.text: Scarcely ___ she opened the envelope when she burst into tears.

questions.explanation: 'That said' (= 'having said that') introduces a point that limits what came before: The hotel is lovely. That said, it's expensive.

wrongReasons.saying: The fixed linker is 'That said', with the past participle.
wrongReasons.says: 'That says' is not a linker; the phrase is 'That said'.

questions.text: The new drug is highly effective. That ___, its side effects remain a serious concern.

questions.explanation: In a present 'What... do' cleft we use 'is (to) + base verb': What you should do is apologise.

wrongReasons.are: The 'What...' clause is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
wrongReasons.does: The cleft links the clause to the focus with 'be', not 'do'.

questions.text: What you need to do ___ ring the bank before they close the account.

questions.explanation: 'Widespread acclaim/praise' means approval from many people: The novel won widespread acclaim.

wrongReasons.applause: 'applause' is clapping at a live event, not critics' written opinions.
wrongReasons.fame: 'fame' is not something critics give; we say 'widespread acclaim'.

questions.text: The museum's new wing has won widespread critical ___.

questions.explanation: 'Provided (that)' means 'only if': Provided that you pay on time, there is no fee.

wrongReasons.if: 'Provided if' combines two conditional words; use 'Provided that'.

questions.text: Provided ___ the weather holds, the concert will go ahead outdoors.

questions.explanation: 'A shot in the dark' / 'shooting in the dark' means guessing without information: My answer was just a shot in the dark.

wrongReasons.night: The idiom is 'in the dark', not 'in the night'.
wrongReasons.air: 'shooting in the air' is literal; the idiom for guessing is 'in the dark'.

questions.text: Launching a product without market research is like shooting in the ___.

questions.explanation: A fronted negative object like 'Not a single word' causes inversion with 'did' in the past: Not one mistake did he make.

wrongReasons.had: 'say' is a base verb, so the auxiliary must be 'did'.
wrongReasons.does: The meal is in the past, so 'does' is the wrong tense.

questions.text: Not a single word ___ she say during the entire meal.

questions.explanation: 'Not because of X but because of Y' contrasts two reasons: He left not because of the pay but because of the hours.

wrongReasons.due: 'due of' is wrong; we say 'due to'. And the parallel structure needs 'because of'.

questions.text: The talks failed, not ___ of a lack of goodwill but because of deep mistrust.

questions.explanation: We use 'that' (or 'which' for things) after the focused element in an 'It was' cleft: It was luck that saved us.

wrongReasons.who: 'her persistence' is not a person, so 'who' is wrong.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun phrase in an 'It was... that' cleft.

questions.text: It was her persistence, more than her talent, ___ won her the scholarship.

questions.explanation: 'Take offence' means to feel upset by something said or done: She took offence at his joke.

wrongReasons.offend: 'offend' is a verb; after 'take' we need the noun 'offence'.
wrongReasons.insult: We 'take something as an insult', but the fixed phrase here is 'take offence'.

questions.text: Please don't take ___ if I suggest a few changes to your report.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional can link a past condition to a present result: Had I left earlier, I wouldn't be stuck now.

wrongReasons.wouldn't have: 'now' shows a present result, so 'wouldn't be', not 'wouldn't have been'.
wrongReasons.won't: The situation is unreal, so 'won't' (real future) is wrong.

questions.text: Had they not signed the contract, they ___ be facing these penalties now.

questions.explanation: 'Back to square one' means back to the beginning after a failure: The plan failed, so we're back to square one.

wrongReasons.zero: The idiom is 'square one', not 'square zero'.
wrongReasons.first: The fixed form is 'square one', not 'square first'.

questions.text: The reporter refused to reveal her source, so the police were back to square ___.

questions.explanation: 'Under no circumstances' is followed by an inverted modal: Under no circumstances must you tell her.

wrongReasons.is: 'is be' is ungrammatical; a modal is needed before 'be'.

questions.text: Under no circumstances ___ the vaccine be stored above eight degrees.

questions.explanation: 'Thus / thereby + -ing' introduces a result of the previous action: She practised daily, thus improving her skills.

wrongReasons.so: 'so' is not followed directly by an -ing clause in this way.
wrongReasons.hence: 'hence' is normally followed by a noun ('hence the delay'), not by an -ing clause.

questions.text: The company has invested heavily in new technology, ___ improving its productivity.

questions.explanation: A 'What' cleft can be followed by 'was + wh-clause': What I don't know is where she lives.

wrongReasons.were: A 'What...' clause takes a singular verb.
wrongReasons.had been: The simple past 'was' is needed to match 'surprised'; a past perfect makes no sense here.

questions.text: What surprised everyone ___ how quickly the rival company copied the idea.

questions.explanation: 'A hot potato' is a controversial issue that people find difficult to deal with: Pension reform is a political hot potato.

wrongReasons.topic: 'hot topic' means a popular subject; 'political hot potato' stresses that it is dangerous to handle.
wrongReasons.issue: 'hot issue' exists, but the fixed expression with 'political hot' is 'hot potato'.

questions.text: Immigration remains a political hot ___ in many European countries.

questions.explanation: 'Even if' means 'whether or not' and stresses that the result does not change: Even if it rains, we'll go.

wrongReasons.unless: 'Even unless' is not a conjunction; to mean 'whether or not' we use 'even if'.
wrongReasons.when: 'even when' refers to repeated times, not one imaginary condition.

questions.text: Even ___ he apologised, I doubt she would forgive him.

questions.explanation: 'A feather in your cap' is an achievement to be proud of: Publishing the paper was a feather in his cap.

wrongReasons.hat: The idiom is 'a feather in your cap', not 'hat'.

questions.text: Winning the contract was a real feather in her ___.

questions.explanation: 'Only then' at the start causes inversion: Only then did he admit the truth.

wrongReasons.I did: After 'Only then', the auxiliary goes before the subject: 'did I'.
wrongReasons.had: 'understand' is a base verb, so we need 'did', not 'had'.

questions.text: Only then ___ I understand why she had kept the letter for so long.

questions.explanation: 'Provided / providing (that)' means 'on condition that': You can come, provided that you're quiet.

wrongReasons.unless: 'unless that' is ungrammatical and reverses the meaning.
wrongReasons.given: 'given that' means 'considering that', not 'on condition that'.

questions.text: The contract can be terminated by either party, ___ that thirty days' notice is given.

questions.explanation: Adverbs like 'precisely' can strengthen the focus in an 'It is... that' cleft: It is precisely this point that I dispute.

wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow the noun phrase 'this lack of transparency'.
wrongReasons.it: Adding 'it' creates a second subject; the cleft needs 'that'.

questions.text: It is precisely this lack of transparency ___ has eroded public trust in the agency.

questions.explanation: 'Launch an investigation/inquiry into something' means to start examining it officially: They launched an inquiry into the accident.

wrongReasons.research: 'research into' is academic study, not a police action.
wrongReasons.search: We 'launch a search for' someone, not 'a search into' a disappearance.

questions.text: Police have launched a full-scale ___ into the disappearance.

questions.explanation: 'In the event of / In case of + noun' are formal ways to say 'if there is': In the event of an emergency, call 999.

wrongReasons.event: The fixed phrase needs the article: 'in the event of'.

questions.text: In ___ of fire, do not use the lifts.

questions.explanation: 'Take something with a pinch (grain) of salt' means not to believe it completely: Take his claims with a pinch of salt.

wrongReasons.sugar: The fixed idiom is 'a pinch of salt'.

questions.text: The CEO's speech was full of empty promises; I'd take it with a pinch of ___.

questions.explanation: 'In no way' means 'not at all' and causes inversion: In no way does this excuse his behaviour.

wrongReasons.do: 'this decision' is singular, so the auxiliary is 'does'.
wrongReasons.is: 'is reflect' is ungrammatical; the auxiliary for the base verb is 'does'.

questions.text: In no way ___ this decision reflect the views of the whole department.

questions.explanation: 'Despite / in spite of + noun' introduces a contrast: The trip was fun despite the weather.

wrongReasons.although: 'although' needs a clause; 'the limited budget' is only a noun phrase.
wrongReasons.however: 'however' is an adverb and cannot introduce a noun phrase like this.

questions.text: The experiment was a success, ___ the limited budget.

questions.explanation: 'All that remains is for + object + to-infinitive' means the only step left: All that remains is for you to sign.

wrongReasons.are: 'All that remains' means 'the only thing left', which is singular.
wrongReasons.was: The sentence describes the present situation, so 'was' is the wrong tense.

questions.text: All that remains ___ for the board to approve the final budget.

questions.explanation: 'Send shock waves through something' means to cause great surprise and worry: The news sent shock waves through the market.

wrongReasons.wave: The phrase uses the plural 'shock waves'.
wrongReasons.shocks: The fixed compound is 'shock waves', not 'shock shocks'.

questions.text: The sudden resignation of the CEO sent shock ___ through the industry.

questions.explanation: The third conditional uses 'if + past perfect'; 'have' becomes 'had had': If I had had time, I would have come.

wrongReasons.had: The result is past (would have called), so the if-clause needs the past perfect 'had had'.
wrongReasons.would have had: 'would' is not used in the if-clause.

questions.text: I would have called you if I ___ your number.

questions.explanation: 'Get cold feet' means to become too nervous to do something you planned: He got cold feet before the wedding.

wrongReasons.hands: The idiom is 'cold feet', not 'cold hands'.
wrongReasons.foot: The idiom always uses the plural 'feet'.

questions.text: I was going to tell him the truth, but I got cold ___ at the last moment.

questions.explanation: 'Rarely' at the start causes inversion with 'do/does/did': Rarely do we see such talent.

wrongReasons.does: 'the two brothers' is plural, so 'does' does not agree.
wrongReasons.are: 'are agree' is ungrammatical; we need 'do' before the base verb.

questions.text: Rarely ___ the two brothers agree on anything, let alone politics.

questions.explanation: 'However / that said' introduces a contrast or limitation to what was just said: I like him; that said, he can be lazy.

wrongReasons.therefore: 'therefore' introduces a result, but the warning contrasts with the forgiveness.
wrongReasons.besides: 'besides' adds a similar point, but here there is a contrast.

questions.text: I'll forgive you this time; ___, there won't be a second chance.

questions.explanation: After 'What I object to is', we put a noun phrase as the focus: What I like is the colour.

wrongReasons.a: We mean one specific manner, so the definite article 'the' is needed.
wrongReasons.how: 'how the way' doubles the idea of manner; use 'the way' or 'how' alone.

questions.text: What I object to is ___ way the decision was announced, not the decision itself.

questions.explanation: 'A period of relative calm/stability/peace' describes a quieter time after trouble: There followed a period of relative calm.

wrongReasons.silent: An adjective cannot follow 'relative' as a noun here; we need a noun.
wrongReasons.quietness: 'quietness' is unusual in this phrase; we say 'relative calm'.

questions.text: After years of conflict, the region is finally enjoying a period of relative ___.

questions.explanation: 'But for + noun' is a formal way of saying 'If it had not been for': But for the rain, we would have won.

wrongReasons.without: 'But without' doubles the negative idea; the fixed phrase is 'But for'.
wrongReasons.of: The fixed phrase is 'But for', not 'But of'.

questions.text: But ___ her quick thinking, the whole building could have burned down.

questions.explanation: 'Be thrown in at the deep end' means to face a difficult task without preparation: New teachers are often thrown in at the deep end.

wrongReasons.water: The idiom is 'the deep end', referring to the deep part of a swimming pool.
wrongReasons.side: The fixed form is 'the deep end', not 'side'.

questions.text: The young lawyer was thrown in at the deep ___ on her first day.

questions.explanation: 'Not only' at the start causes inversion; 'but also' introduces the second point: Not only did he lie, but he also stole.

wrongReasons.has: 'lose' is a base verb and the second clause is past, so 'did' is needed.

questions.text: Not only ___ the company lose money, but it also damaged its reputation.

questions.explanation: A comment clause with ', which' refers back to the whole previous clause: He was late, which annoyed everyone.

wrongReasons.that: 'that' cannot follow a comma to comment on a whole clause.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot refer back to a previous clause; we use 'which'.

questions.text: The village is accessible only by boat, ___ makes deliveries extremely costly.

questions.explanation: Negative clefts use 'It was not until... that...': It was not until later that I saw the problem.

wrongReasons.before: 'before' changes the structure; the fixed cleft is 'not until... that'.
wrongReasons.so: 'so' cannot introduce the second part of this cleft.

questions.text: It was not until she had lived abroad ___ she truly appreciated her own language.

questions.explanation: 'Have a good/excellent/fluent command of a language' means to speak it very well: He has an excellent command of French.

wrongReasons.high: 'high command' refers to military leaders, not language skills.
wrongReasons.big: 'big command' is not a natural collocation.

questions.text: She has a ___ command of four languages, including Mandarin.

questions.explanation: 'If you happen to' adds the idea of chance to a conditional: If you happen to pass a shop, buy some milk.

wrongReasons.for: 'happen' is followed by 'to + base verb', not 'for'.
wrongReasons.seeing: 'happen' is followed by the to-infinitive, so 'happen seeing' is wrong.

questions.text: If you happen ___ see Clara at the conference, give her my regards.

questions.explanation: 'A bitter pill to swallow' is an unpleasant fact you have to accept: Losing the final was a bitter pill to swallow.

wrongReasons.medicine: We say 'a taste of your own medicine' elsewhere, but the idiom here is 'a bitter pill'.
wrongReasons.fruit: 'bitter fruit' is not the idiom for accepting bad news.

questions.text: Selling the family business was a bitter ___ to swallow for my grandfather.

questions.explanation: 'Nowhere' at the start causes inversion: Nowhere is the air cleaner than here.

wrongReasons.is: The subject 'the effects' is plural, so 'are', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.do: There is no main verb after 'more visible', so 'do' cannot be used; we need 'are'.

questions.text: Nowhere ___ the effects of climate change more visible than in the Arctic.

questions.explanation: 'Despite the fact that + clause' introduces a contrast: Despite the fact that it rained, we enjoyed it.

wrongReasons.although: 'Although the fact that' is wrong; 'although' is followed directly by a clause.
wrongReasons.in spite: We need 'In spite of the fact that'; 'in spite' alone is incomplete.

questions.text: ___ the fact that he had no formal training, he became a respected architect.

questions.explanation: A 'Why' clause as subject is singular: Why he left has never been clear.

wrongReasons.have: A 'Why...' clause acts as a singular subject, so 'have' does not agree.
wrongReasons.was: 'never been' needs the auxiliary 'has' (present perfect), not 'was'.

questions.text: Why they chose such a remote location ___ never been fully explained.

questions.explanation: 'Run into / meet with fierce opposition/resistance' means to be strongly opposed: The reform ran into fierce opposition.

wrongReasons.disagreement: 'fierce disagreement' exists between people, but 'run into fierce' goes with 'opposition' or 'resistance'.
wrongReasons.refusal: 'refusal' is not used with 'run into fierce'.

questions.text: The plan to build a motorway through the valley ran into fierce ___ from farmers.

questions.explanation: 'Were + subject + to + verb' expresses an unlikely future condition: Were he to win, it would be a miracle.

wrongReasons.for: The inverted conditional uses 'Were... to', not 'for'.
wrongReasons.going to: 'going to' is not used in this inverted structure.

questions.text: Were the government ___ raise taxes again, it would face widespread protest.

questions.explanation: 'Back to the drawing board' means you must start planning again: The test failed — back to the drawing board.

wrongReasons.table: The idiom is 'drawing board', not 'drawing table'.
wrongReasons.paper: The fixed form is 'the drawing board'.

questions.text: The architect's plans were rejected, so it's back to the drawing ___.

questions.explanation: 'At no point' at the start causes inversion: At no point did I feel unsafe.

wrongReasons.had: 'admit' is a base verb, so we need 'did'.

questions.text: At no point ___ the suspect admit to being at the scene.

questions.explanation: 'So that' can show a result or purpose: The text was encrypted so that nobody else could read it.

wrongReasons.as: 'as that' is not a linker; to show a result we use 'so that'.
wrongReasons.for: 'for that' cannot introduce a result clause; we need 'so that'.

questions.text: The documents were written in code, ___ that only a few officials could read them.

questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on the advice of someone', here placed in the focus of an 'It was... that' cleft: It was on my advice that he waited.

wrongReasons.by: We do not say 'by the advice of'; the collocation is 'on the advice of'.
wrongReasons.with: 'with the advice of' is not the fixed phrase; use 'on the advice of'.

questions.text: It was ___ the advice of her lawyer that she declined to comment.

questions.explanation: 'Pull your (own) weight' means to do your fair share of the work: Everyone has to pull their weight.

wrongReasons.carry: We 'carry' a heavy load, but the fixed phrase is 'pull your weight'.
wrongReasons.lift: 'lift your weight' describes exercise, not doing your share.

questions.text: You will need to ___ your own weight if you want to stay on this team.

questions.explanation: A mixed conditional: past condition (if + past perfect) and present result (would + base verb): If I hadn't eaten so much, I wouldn't feel sick.

wrongReasons.didn't: The staying up happened last night, so the past perfect 'hadn't stayed' is needed.
wrongReasons.wouldn't have: 'would' does not go in the if-clause.

questions.text: I wouldn't be so tired today if I ___ stayed up watching that film.

questions.explanation: 'Not hold water' means an argument or theory is not convincing: Her excuse doesn't hold water.

wrongReasons.weight: We say an argument 'carries weight', but for being logically sound we say 'hold water'.
wrongReasons.ground: 'hold its ground' means to refuse to retreat; it does not describe whether an explanation is convincing.

questions.text: His explanation doesn't hold ___; the timings simply don't add up.

questions.explanation: 'Only when + clause' causes inversion in the main clause: Only when it's dark can you see the stars.

wrongReasons.you will: After 'Only when...', the auxiliary goes before the subject: 'will you'.
wrongReasons.would: The sentence describes a general truth or future, not an unreal situation, so 'would' does not fit.

questions.text: Only when you have tried it yourself ___ you appreciate how hard it is.

questions.explanation: 'At times' means 'sometimes': The film is, at times, very moving.

wrongReasons.time: The phrase uses the plural: 'at times'.

questions.text: The novel is long and, at ___, rather difficult to follow.

questions.explanation: A reversed 'What' cleft puts the focus first: The delay is what upsets people.

wrongReasons.that: Without a noun before it, 'that' cannot mean 'the thing which'; use 'what'.
wrongReasons.which: 'which' needs an antecedent noun; 'what' includes it.

questions.text: Not the cost but the delay is ___ really frustrates passengers.

questions.explanation: 'The full/true extent of something' means how big or serious it really is: We do not yet know the full extent of the problem.

wrongReasons.whole: 'the whole extent' is unnatural; we say 'the full extent'.
wrongReasons.complete: 'complete extent' is rare; the natural collocation is 'full' or 'true'.

questions.text: Few people realise the ___ extent of the damage caused by the storm.

questions.explanation: 'Unless otherwise stated/indicated' is a formal reduced conditional meaning 'if nothing different is said': Unless otherwise stated, the meeting starts at nine.

wrongReasons.saying: The reduced clause is passive ('unless it is otherwise stated'), so we need a past participle, not '-ing'.
wrongReasons.state: After 'Unless otherwise' we need the past participle 'stated', not the base form.

questions.text: Unless otherwise ___, all prices include local taxes.

questions.explanation: 'Make a mountain out of a molehill' means to treat a small problem as very serious: Stop making a mountain out of a molehill.

wrongReasons.hill: The idiom is 'molehill', the small pile of earth made by a mole.
wrongReasons.stone: The fixed form is 'out of a molehill'.

questions.text: The opposition is making a mountain out of a ___ over a minor spending error.

questions.explanation: After adverbs of place or direction like 'Down', 'Out' or 'Up', a verb of movement can come before a noun subject: Down came the snow.

wrongReasons.did come: With this kind of inversion we use the main verb itself, not 'did'.
wrongReasons.comes: The match was abandoned in the past, so the verb must be 'came'.

questions.text: Down ___ the rain, and the match had to be abandoned.

questions.explanation: 'Regardless / irrespective of' means 'without being affected by': Regardless of the cost, we will go.

wrongReasons.despite: 'Despite of' is wrong, and 'despite' does not mean 'whatever'.
wrongReasons.irregardless: 'irregardless' is not standard English and is avoided in formal English.

questions.text: ___ of how long it takes, we must find the source of the leak.

questions.explanation: In 'What matters is + whether/how/if-clause' the verb is singular: What matters is how you finish.

wrongReasons.are: A 'What...' clause is singular, so 'are' does not agree.
wrongReasons.was: 'matters' is present, so the cleft verb should be present too.

questions.text: What matters most in this case ___ whether the witness can be considered reliable.

questions.explanation: 'Bear a (striking) resemblance to' means to look very similar: She bears a striking resemblance to her aunt.

wrongReasons.resemble: 'resemble' is a verb; after 'a striking' we need the noun 'resemblance'.
wrongReasons.similar: 'similar' is an adjective; after 'a striking' we need a noun.

questions.text: The artist's early work bears a striking ___ to that of Matisse.

questions.explanation: 'In case' means 'as a precaution against the possibility that': I'll take a map in case we get lost.

wrongReasons.event: 'In event it rains' is wrong; 'in the event that' needs 'the' and 'that'.
wrongReasons.if: 'in if' is not a phrase; use 'in case'.

questions.text: Take an umbrella in ___ it rains later.

questions.explanation: 'Beat about (around) the bush' means to avoid saying something directly: Stop beating about the bush and tell me.

wrongReasons.house: The fixed form is 'beat about the bush'.

questions.text: I'm not going to beat about the ___: your work this term has been unacceptable.

questions.explanation: After 'Here' or 'There', a noun subject follows the verb: Here comes the train.

wrongReasons.come: 'the bus' is singular, so the verb is 'comes'.
wrongReasons.is coming: With 'Here' inversion we use the present simple, not the continuous.

questions.text: Here ___ the bus at last — we've been waiting for forty minutes!

questions.explanation: 'Albeit / though / although + adjective' adds a concession without a full clause: It was a success, albeit a small one.

wrongReasons.despite: 'despite' must be followed by a noun or -ing form, not a bare adjective.
wrongReasons.however: 'however incomplete' would mean 'no matter how incomplete', which changes the meaning.

questions.text: The data, ___ incomplete, point to a clear upward trend.

questions.explanation: We can focus a manner phrase in an 'It was... that' cleft: It was by mistake that I deleted it.

wrongReasons.how: 'how' cannot introduce the second part of an 'It was... that' cleft.
wrongReasons.which: 'which' refers to a noun, but 'by sheer chance' is an adverbial phrase.

questions.text: It was by sheer chance ___ the archaeologists discovered the burial chamber.

questions.explanation: 'Voter turnout' is the number of people who vote: Turnout was high in the cities.

wrongReasons.attendance: 'attendance' is for events or school; for elections we say 'turnout'.
wrongReasons.presence: 'presence' means being somewhere, not the number of people who vote.

questions.text: Voter ___ was unusually low, with only 38% of the electorate casting a ballot.

questions.explanation: The third conditional uses 'if + had + past participle': If they had trained harder, they might have won.

wrongReasons.has: The event is in the past, so 'has' (present perfect) is wrong.
wrongReasons.would: 'would' is not used in the if-clause.

questions.text: If the goalkeeper ___ not been injured, we might have won the final.

questions.explanation: 'The game is up' means a secret plan or deception has been discovered: The game's up — the police know everything.

wrongReasons.time: 'time is up' means there is no time left, not that a deception is discovered.
wrongReasons.play: The fixed idiom is 'the game is up'.

questions.text: When the auditors arrived, the manager knew the ___ was up.

questions.explanation: 'Not once' at the start causes inversion: Not once has she complained.

wrongReasons.did: 'thanked' is a past participle here, so the auxiliary must be 'has' or 'had'.

questions.text: Not once ___ he thanked me for all the help I gave him.

questions.explanation: 'Owing to / due to + noun' gives a reason: The match was cancelled owing to rain.

wrongReasons.because: 'because to' is wrong; we say 'because of'.
wrongReasons.thanks: 'thanks to' usually suggests a positive cause; a staff shortage is negative.

questions.text: The report was delayed, ___ to a shortage of qualified staff.

questions.explanation: 'Something that...' can begin a pseudo-cleft: Something that helps is regular sleep.

wrongReasons.what: 'Something what' is ungrammatical; after 'something' use 'that' or 'which'.

questions.text: Something ___ often goes unnoticed is the role of volunteers in disaster relief.

questions.explanation: We 'accept/take/assume responsibility for something': She took full responsibility for the error.

wrongReasons.make: 'make responsibility' is not an English collocation.
wrongReasons.do: 'do responsibility' is not used; we 'take' or 'accept' it.

questions.text: The CEO refused to ___ responsibility for the data breach.

questions.explanation: 'Assuming (that)' introduces a real condition and is followed by a present tense for the future: Assuming it stops raining, we'll walk.

wrongReasons.will arrive: After conditional words like 'Assuming', we use the present for the future, not 'will'.
wrongReasons.arrived: The main clause uses 'will', so this is a real condition; the past 'arrived' is wrong.

questions.text: Assuming the shipment ___ on time, the shop will reopen next Monday.

questions.explanation: 'Find your feet' means to become confident in a new situation: It took her a while to find her feet at university.

wrongReasons.foot: The idiom always uses the plural: 'find your feet'.
wrongReasons.legs: We say 'find your sea legs' on a ship, but the general idiom is 'find your feet'.

questions.text: The start-up is still finding its ___ after only six months on the market.

questions.explanation: 'Only in + time' at the start causes inversion: Only in recent years have prices fallen.

wrongReasons.did: 'begun' is a past participle, so the auxiliary must be 'have'.

questions.text: Only in the last decade ___ researchers begun to understand the disease.

questions.explanation: 'Nevertheless / even so' introduce a contrast with the previous statement: It was cheap; even so, I didn't buy it.

wrongReasons.therefore: 'therefore' shows a result, but donations being welcome is a contrast to free entry.
wrongReasons.otherwise: 'otherwise' means 'if not', which makes no sense here.

questions.text: The museum is free to enter; ___, donations are always welcome.

questions.explanation: 'The person who/that...' is a common cleft-like structure; the preposition can stay at the end: The person I owe most to is my mother.

wrongReasons.which: 'which' is for things; 'the person' needs 'who', 'whom' or 'that'.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun like 'the person'.

questions.text: The person ___ I owe my career to is my first piano teacher.

questions.explanation: 'Go to great lengths to do something' means to make a big effort: She went to great lengths to find him.

wrongReasons.length: The fixed phrase uses the plural 'lengths'.
wrongReasons.efforts: We 'make great efforts', but the verb 'go to' collocates with 'great lengths'.

questions.text: The company went to great ___ to protect its customers' privacy.

questions.explanation: 'It's high time + subject + past simple' means it should happen now: It's high time you went to bed.

wrongReasons.does: After 'It's high time', we use the past simple even though we mean the present.
wrongReasons.will do: 'will' is not used after 'It's high time'.

questions.text: It's high time the council ___ something about the potholes on this road.

questions.explanation: 'Walk on eggshells' means to be very careful not to upset someone: We all walk on eggshells around him.

wrongReasons.glass: 'walk on broken glass' is not the idiom; we say 'walk on eggshells'.
wrongReasons.ice: 'on thin ice' means in a risky position, not being careful with someone's feelings.

questions.text: Everyone in the office is walking on ___ since the director's outburst.

questions.explanation: 'Much as + subject + verb' means 'although... very much': Much as I like him, I don't trust him.

wrongReasons.so: 'Much so' is not a concessive linker.

questions.text: Much ___ I admire her courage, I cannot support her decision.

questions.explanation: 'Not that + clause' adds a comment that limits or corrects what follows: Not that it matters, but I was right.

wrongReasons.because: 'Not because' gives a reason; 'Not that' introduces a polite qualification.
wrongReasons.if: 'Not if you need' does not form a complete idea here.

questions.text: Not ___ you need any help, but would you like me to check your figures?

questions.explanation: 'It's not that... it's (just) that...' corrects a possible misunderstanding: It's not that I'm angry, it's that I'm tired.

wrongReasons.because: The fixed pattern is 'It's not that... it's just that'; 'because' breaks the parallel.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot introduce a complete clause after 'it's just'.

questions.text: It's not that I dislike modern art; it's just ___ I don't understand most of it.

questions.explanation: 'Take something out of context' means to quote it without its surroundings so its meaning changes: My words were taken out of context.

wrongReasons.contest: 'contest' means a competition; the phrase is 'out of context'.
wrongReasons.content: 'content' means what is inside something; the phrase is 'out of context'.

questions.text: His comments were taken out of ___ and widely misreported.

questions.explanation: In an inverted third conditional, 'Had' is followed by the past participle: Had I known, I would have stayed.

wrongReasons.knew: After 'Had' we need the past participle 'known', not the past simple.
wrongReasons.know: After 'Had' we need the past participle, not the base form.

questions.text: Had I ___ how difficult the course was, I would never have enrolled.

questions.explanation: 'The talk of the town' is something everyone is discussing: Their wedding was the talk of the town.

wrongReasons.village: The fixed form is 'the talk of the town'.

questions.text: The new curfew rule was the talk of the ___ for weeks.

questions.explanation: 'So + adjective + be + subject + that' is an emphatic inversion: So strong was the wind that trees fell.

wrongReasons.is: 'dried up' is past, so the verb must be 'was'.
wrongReasons.were: 'the drought' is singular, so 'were' does not agree.

questions.text: So severe ___ the drought that the river dried up completely.

questions.explanation: 'Much to + someone's + emotion' expresses a feeling caused by an event: Much to my surprise, she agreed.

wrongReasons.for: The fixed phrase is 'much to the disappointment of', not 'for'.
wrongReasons.by: 'much by' is not a linking phrase.

questions.text: The festival was cancelled, much ___ the disappointment of local businesses.

questions.explanation: 'What happened was (that) + clause' introduces an event in a narrative: What happened was that the bus broke down.

wrongReasons.is: The story is in the past (happened, crashed), so use 'was'.

questions.text: What happened ___ that the server crashed in the middle of the presentation.

questions.explanation: 'Paint a rosy picture' means to describe something as better than it is; 'far from rosy' means quite bad: The outlook is far from rosy.

wrongReasons.red: 'red' does not suggest optimism; the fixed phrase is 'a rosy picture'.

questions.text: The latest figures paint a far from ___ picture of the economy.

questions.explanation: 'Suppose' with an imaginary future situation takes the past simple: Suppose you met the president, what would you say?

wrongReasons.win: With 'would' in the result, the imaginary condition needs a past form ('won').
wrongReasons.will win: 'will' is not used after 'Suppose' in a conditional.

questions.text: Suppose you ___ the lottery tomorrow, would you give up your job?

questions.explanation: 'A stroke of luck' is an unexpected piece of good fortune: By a stroke of luck, the shop was still open.

wrongReasons.hit: We say 'a stroke of luck', not 'a hit of luck'.
wrongReasons.piece: 'a piece of luck' is rare; the standard phrase is 'a stroke of luck'.

questions.text: Passing the exam without studying was a real ___ of luck.

questions.explanation: 'Adjective + as/though + subject + verb' is a concessive inversion meaning 'although it may seem strange': Tired as she was, she kept going.

wrongReasons.so: 'Strange so it may seem' is not a concessive structure; we use 'as' or 'though'.

questions.text: Strange ___ it may seem, the shy boy became a famous comedian.

questions.explanation: 'Otherwise / or else' means 'if we do not': Hurry up, otherwise we'll miss the train.

wrongReasons.unless: 'unless' would mean we risk losing it only if we do not risk it, which is illogical.
wrongReasons.however: 'however' introduces a contrast, not the consequence of not acting.

questions.text: We must act now, ___ we risk losing the contract altogether.

questions.explanation: 'rather than' can contrast two elements inside the focus of a cleft: It was the music, rather than the food, that people liked.

wrongReasons.who: 'the smell of the sea' is not a person, so 'who' is wrong.
wrongReasons.what: 'what' cannot follow a noun phrase in an 'It was... that' cleft.

questions.text: It was the smell of the sea, rather than the view, ___ brought back her childhood.

questions.explanation: 'Behind closed doors' means in private: The meeting took place behind closed doors.

wrongReasons.door: The fixed phrase always uses the plural 'doors'.
wrongReasons.curtains: 'behind closed curtains' is not the idiom for private meetings.

questions.text: The two leaders held talks behind closed ___ for over six hours.

questions.explanation: 'If only + past perfect' expresses regret about the past: If only I had studied harder.

wrongReasons.have: The regret is about the past (when I was younger), so 'had listened' is needed.
wrongReasons.would have: 'If only I would have' is not standard; use 'If only I had'.

questions.text: If only I ___ listened to my grandmother's advice when I was younger.

questions.explanation: 'Be at loggerheads (with)' and 'be at odds' mean to disagree strongly: The neighbours have been at loggerheads for years.

wrongReasons.war: 'at war' is literal and too strong for a political disagreement.
wrongReasons.heads: The idiom is 'at loggerheads', not 'at heads'.

questions.text: The two parties are at ___ over the new immigration bill.

questions.explanation: 'Only if + clause' at the start causes inversion in the main clause: Only if you apologise will she forgive you.

wrongReasons.the proposal will: After 'Only if...', the auxiliary goes before the subject.
wrongReasons.does: 'does be adopted' is ungrammatical; a modal is needed before 'be'.

questions.text: Only if all members agree ___ the proposal be adopted.

questions.explanation: After 'to have' we need the past participle 'been' to form the perfect passive infinitive: It is believed to have been stolen.

wrongReasons.being: 'to have being' is not a verb form; after 'have' we need the participle 'been'.
wrongReasons.be: 'to have be' is ungrammatical; the perfect infinitive uses 'have been'.

questions.text: The manuscript is believed to have ___ smuggled out of the country during the war.

questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is 'is being' + past participle, for actions in progress now: The road is being repaired.

wrongReasons.been: 'is been' is not English; 'as we speak' needs the continuous form 'is being reviewed'.
wrongReasons.be: 'is be reviewed' has two finite verbs; the continuous passive is 'is being reviewed'.

questions.text: The decision to close the factory is ___ reviewed by the board as we speak.

questions.explanation: After verbs like 'hate', 'like' and 'resent' the passive gerund is 'being' + past participle: He hates being ignored.

wrongReasons.be: 'hate' is followed by a gerund here, so the passive form is 'being told', not 'be told'.
wrongReasons.to be: 'hate to be told' is possible in general, but the gap takes one word: the passive gerund 'being'.

questions.text: She hates ___ told what to do by people half her age.

questions.explanation: Modal perfect passive = modal + have been + past participle: It should have been done earlier.

wrongReasons.be: 'should have be' is ungrammatical; use 'should have been checked'.

questions.text: The results should have ___ checked before they were published.

questions.explanation: 'Be said / believed / thought' is followed by a to-infinitive: The castle is said to be haunted.

wrongReasons.that: 'is said that' needs the subject 'It' (It is said that...); with a personal subject use 'is said to'.

questions.text: The ancient city is said ___ have been destroyed by an earthquake in the fourth century.

questions.explanation: Future passive = will be / is going to be + past participle: The results will be announced tomorrow.

wrongReasons.will: 'will opened' lacks 'be'; the future passive is 'will be opened'.
wrongReasons.opens: The wing does not open itself here; the mayor opens it, so we need a passive form such as 'will be opened'.

questions.text: The new wing of the hospital ___ opened by the mayor next Friday.

questions.explanation: 'Get + object + past participle' can describe something unpleasant that happens to you: She got her car stolen.

wrongReasons.reject: After 'get + object' we need the past participle 'rejected', not the base form.
wrongReasons.rejecting: The application did not reject anything; it was rejected, so use the past participle.

questions.text: He got his visa application ___ on a technicality, which meant he had to start all over again.

questions.explanation: Causative 'have something done' = arrange for someone else to do it: I had my hair cut.

wrongReasons.repair: 'have the roof repair' uses the base form; the causative needs the past participle 'repaired'.
wrongReasons.repairing: 'have the roof repairing' is wrong; someone else repairs it, so use 'have it repaired'.

questions.text: We need to have the roof ___ before the winter storms arrive.

questions.explanation: Past perfect passive = had been + past participle: The letter had been opened.

wrongReasons.being: 'had long being' is not a verb form; use 'had been presumed'.
wrongReasons.was: 'had was' combines two auxiliaries wrongly; the past perfect passive is 'had been'.

questions.text: The painting, which had long ___ presumed lost, turned up in an attic in Ghent.

questions.explanation: For an earlier action, use 'be alleged / said / thought' + perfect infinitive 'to have' + past participle: He is said to have fled.

wrongReasons.to: 'to laundered' mixes an infinitive with a past participle; we need 'to have laundered'.
wrongReasons.having: 'be alleged' is followed by a to-infinitive, not a gerund: 'are alleged to have laundered'.

questions.text: The suspects are alleged ___ laundered millions through a network of shell companies.

questions.explanation: Impersonal passive with a modal of possibility: It could be argued that... introduces a cautious opinion.

wrongReasons.is: 'It is be argued' has two finite verbs; use a modal: 'It could be argued'.
wrongReasons.has: 'It has be argued' is ungrammatical; we need a modal + 'be argued'.

questions.text: It ___ be argued that the reforms did more harm than good.

questions.explanation: Past perfect passive shows an action completed before another past event: The food had been eaten.

wrongReasons.be: After 'had' we need the participle 'been', not 'be'.
wrongReasons.being: 'had already being' is not English; the correct form is 'had already been destroyed'.

questions.text: By the time the firefighters arrived, most of the building had already ___ destroyed.

questions.explanation: 'Be required' is followed by a to-infinitive: Staff are required to wear badges.

wrongReasons.for: 'be required for' is followed by a noun, not a verb; before 'submit' we need 'to'.
wrongReasons.of: 'required of' is used as in 'what is required of you'; before a verb we need 'to'.

questions.text: Under the new rules, every applicant will be required ___ submit two references.

questions.explanation: The fixed passive phrase is 'be met with' (= receive a reaction): The plan was met with silence.
