wrongReasons.by: 'met by' is used for people meeting someone (met by a driver); for a reaction we say 'met with'.
wrongReasons.from: 'met from' is not a collocation; a reaction is 'met with'.

questions.text: The proposal was met ___ fierce opposition from local residents.

questions.explanation: Third-conditional passive: could have been + past participle: The accident could have been prevented.

wrongReasons.avoid: After 'have been' we need the past participle 'avoided'.
wrongReasons.avoiding: 'could have been avoiding' is an active continuous form; damage is avoided, so use the participle.

questions.text: Much of the damage could have been ___ if the warnings had been heeded.

questions.explanation: Prepositional verbs keep their preposition at the end in the passive: The lock had been tampered with.

wrongReasons.tamper: After 'were' the passive needs the participle 'tampered'.
wrongReasons.tampering: 'were tampering with' would mean the boxes did the tampering; use the passive 'were tampered with'.

questions.text: There is no evidence that the ballot boxes were ever ___ with.

questions.explanation: Active 'make someone do' has no 'to', but the passive needs it: They were made to wait.

wrongReasons.for: 'made for' does not introduce a verb; the passive pattern is 'be made to + verb'.
wrongReasons.into: 'made into' means 'changed into'; to express being forced, use 'were made to leave'.

questions.text: The tenants were made ___ leave the building within forty-eight hours.

questions.explanation: 'Every' + singular noun takes a singular verb: Every effort is being made.

wrongReasons.are: 'Every precaution' is singular, so the verb is 'is', not 'are'.
wrongReasons.has: 'has being taken' is not a verb form; the continuous passive is 'is being taken'.

questions.text: Every precaution ___ being taken to ensure the safety of the delegates.

questions.explanation: 'Put off / put back' (= postpone) keeps its particle in the passive: The match was put off.

wrongReasons.away: 'put away' means to store something, not to postpone it.
wrongReasons.down: 'put down' means to write or to criticise; postponing is 'put off'.

questions.text: The board meeting has been put ___ until the chairman returns from Tokyo.

questions.explanation: The perfect passive participle 'having been' + past participle shows an earlier passive action: Having been told, she left.

wrongReasons.be: 'Having be warned' is ungrammatical; we need 'having been'.
wrongReasons.being: 'Having being' is not a form; the perfect participle is 'having been'.

questions.text: Having ___ warned twice, the driver had no excuse for ignoring the signal.

questions.explanation: 'Appear / seem' + perfect infinitive refers to an earlier event: He seems to have left.

wrongReasons.to: 'appears to been' is wrong; after 'to' we need 'have been'.
wrongReasons.having: 'appear' takes a to-infinitive, not a gerund: 'appears to have been damaged'.

questions.text: The sculpture appears ___ been damaged in transit.

questions.explanation: 'Look after' (= take care of) keeps its preposition in the passive: The dog is looked after by a neighbour.

wrongReasons.for: 'looked for' means searched for, which does not fit a carer's role.
wrongReasons.at: 'looked at' means observed, not cared for.

questions.text: The twins were looked ___ by their grandmother while their parents worked abroad.

questions.explanation: 'Currently' signals an action in progress, so use the present continuous passive: is being + past participle.

wrongReasons.been: 'is currently been' is ungrammatical; use 'is being tested'.
wrongReasons.be: 'is be tested' has two finite verbs; the continuous passive is 'is being tested'.

questions.text: The new vaccine is currently ___ tested on volunteers in three countries.

questions.explanation: 'Have yet to' + infinitive means 'has not happened so far'; the passive is 'has yet to be explained'.

wrongReasons.to: 'has yet to fully explained' lacks 'be'; the passive needs 'to be explained'.
wrongReasons.being: 'has yet' is followed by a to-infinitive, so 'being' is wrong here.

questions.text: The phenomenon has yet ___ fully explained by scientists.

questions.explanation: Future passive negative: will not be + past participle: Late entries will not be accepted.

wrongReasons.being: After 'will not' we need the base form 'be', not 'being'.
wrongReasons.been: 'will not been' is ungrammatical; use 'will not be considered'.

questions.text: Applicants who fail to meet the deadline will not ___ considered.

questions.explanation: 'Be reported to be + -ing' describes something in progress now: She is said to be living abroad.

wrongReasons.have: 'to have being treated' is not a form; for a current action use 'to be being treated'.
wrongReasons.been: 'to been' is ungrammatical; the infinitive needs 'be'.

questions.text: The hostages are reported to ___ being treated well by their captors.

questions.explanation: Present perfect passive = have been + past participle: The keys have not been found.

wrongReasons.recover: After 'have been' we need the past participle 'recovered'.
wrongReasons.recovering: The jewels cannot recover anything; they are recovered, so use the past participle.

questions.text: The stolen jewels have never been ___, despite a generous reward being offered.

questions.explanation: 'Resent' takes a gerund, so the passive form is 'being' + past participle: He resented being criticised.

wrongReasons.be: 'resent' is followed by a gerund, so 'be passed' is wrong; say 'being passed over'.
wrongReasons.to be: 'resent' is not followed by a to-infinitive; use the gerund 'being'.

questions.text: She resented ___ passed over for promotion yet again.

questions.explanation: Reduced passive clause: 'once (it was) set in motion'. 'Set' is irregular: set – set – set.

wrongReasons.setted: 'set' is irregular; its past participle is 'set', not 'setted'.
wrongReasons.sat: 'sat' is the participle of 'sit'; the collocation is 'set in motion'.

questions.text: The rumour, once ___ in motion, proved impossible to stop.

questions.explanation: 'Be cut off' means to be isolated: The island was cut off by the storm.

wrongReasons.out: 'cut out' means to remove or stop doing something, not to isolate.
wrongReasons.away: 'cut away' means to remove a part by cutting; isolation is 'cut off'.

questions.text: The mountain village is cut ___ whenever heavy snow blocks the pass.

questions.explanation: 'Be regarded as' + noun phrase: He is regarded as an expert.

wrongReasons.like: 'regarded like' is wrong; the verb 'regard' always takes 'as'.
wrongReasons.to be: 'regard' is not followed by 'to be'; the pattern is 'be regarded as'.

questions.text: Despite her youth, she is widely regarded ___ the finest violinist of her generation.

questions.explanation: 'Put / bring something into effect' becomes 'be put into effect' in the passive.

wrongReasons.putted: 'put' is irregular; its past participle is 'put', not 'putted'.
wrongReasons.come: 'come into effect' is intransitive and cannot follow 'be'; the passive is 'be put into effect'.

questions.text: The new tax will be ___ into effect on the first of April.

questions.explanation: 'Bring something to light' (= reveal) in the passive is 'be brought to light'.

wrongReasons.came: 'came' is an active past form and cannot follow 'was'; the passive is 'was brought to light'.

questions.text: Not until the 1990s was the true extent of the fraud finally ___ to light.

questions.explanation: 'Be kept in the dark' (= not be told) is a fixed passive expression.

wrongReasons.on: The idiom is 'in the dark', not 'on the dark'.
wrongReasons.at: 'at the dark' is not English; the idiom uses 'in'.

questions.text: Nobody likes to be kept ___ the dark about decisions that affect their jobs.

questions.explanation: 'Be thought + to have been' refers to a situation that started earlier: They are thought to have met in Paris.

wrongReasons.be: 'to be been' is ungrammatical; the perfect infinitive is 'to have been'.
wrongReasons.had: After 'to' we need the base form 'have', not 'had'.

questions.text: The two firms are thought to ___ been in secret talks for several months.

questions.explanation: 'Break down' (of talks) means to fail and stop: Negotiations broke down at midnight.

wrongReasons.up: 'break up' is used for relationships or crowds, not for failed talks.
wrongReasons.out: 'break out' means to start suddenly (a war, a fire), the opposite idea.

questions.text: The pay talks broke ___ after the unions rejected the final offer.

questions.explanation: 'Iron out' means to solve small problems or difficulties: We need to iron out a few details.

wrongReasons.off: 'iron off' is not a phrasal verb in English.
wrongReasons.away: 'iron away' does not exist; the phrasal verb for removing problems is 'iron out'.

questions.text: It took the developers months to iron ___ all the bugs in the software.

questions.explanation: 'Add up' (informal) means to make sense or seem true: Her story just doesn't add up.

wrongReasons.on: 'add on' means to include something extra, not to make sense.
wrongReasons.together: 'add together' means to calculate a total; it does not mean 'be believable'.

questions.text: I can't quite put my finger on it, but something about his alibi doesn't add ___.

questions.explanation: 'Blow over' means to pass without serious effect: The storm soon blew over.

wrongReasons.up: 'blow up' means to explode or suddenly become serious, the opposite of what everyone hoped.
wrongReasons.away: 'blow away' means to be carried off by wind, or to impress greatly.

questions.text: Everyone hoped the row would blow ___ quickly, but it dominated the headlines for weeks.

questions.explanation: 'Nod off' means to fall asleep unintentionally: Grandpa nodded off in his chair.

wrongReasons.out: 'nod out' is not standard English for falling asleep.
wrongReasons.down: 'nod down' is not a phrasal verb; falling asleep is 'nod off'.

questions.text: She was so exhausted that she nodded ___ in the middle of the lecture.

questions.explanation: 'Gloss over' means to treat something briefly to hide how serious it is: He glossed over his mistakes.

wrongReasons.up: 'gloss up' is not used with this meaning.
wrongReasons.out: 'gloss out' does not exist; the phrasal verb is 'gloss over'.

questions.text: The government has been accused of trying to gloss ___ the scale of the problem.

questions.explanation: 'Fob someone off (with something)' means to satisfy them with something inferior or untrue.

wrongReasons.out: 'fob out' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.away: 'fob away' does not exist; the expression is 'fob someone off'.

questions.text: He tried to fob me ___ with a feeble excuse about the traffic.

questions.explanation: 'Rein in' means to control or limit something: The bank must rein in its lending.

wrongReasons.on: 'rein on' is not English; the phrasal verb is 'rein in'.
wrongReasons.down: 'rein down' does not exist; we limit spending by reining it in.

questions.text: We'll have to rein ___ spending if we want to stay within this year's budget.

questions.explanation: 'Pore over' means to study something very carefully: She pored over the map.

wrongReasons.on: 'pore on' is not used; the correct particle is 'over'.
wrongReasons.into: 'pore into' does not exist; you 'pore over' a document.

questions.text: The lawyer pored ___ the contract for hours, looking for loopholes.

questions.explanation: 'Own up (to something)' means to admit a fault: Nobody owned up to breaking the window.

wrongReasons.on: 'own on' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.out: 'own out' does not exist; admitting guilt is 'own up'.

questions.text: After weeks of denial, the senator finally owned ___ to having misled the committee.

questions.explanation: 'Mull over' means to think carefully about something for a time: Let me mull it over.

wrongReasons.on: 'mull on' is not standard; the phrasal verb is 'mull over'.

questions.text: The committee will mull ___ the proposals before making a decision.

questions.explanation: 'Put someone off' means to make them dislike or lose interest in something.

wrongReasons.out: 'put someone out' means to inconvenience them, not to make them dislike someone.
wrongReasons.down: 'put someone down' means to criticise or humiliate them.

questions.text: Don't let his gruff manner put you ___; he's actually very kind.

questions.explanation: 'Seize on/upon' means to use something eagerly to your advantage: The press seized on the error.

wrongReasons.at: 'seize at' is not the phrasal verb; you seize on an opportunity or mistake.

questions.text: The opposition seized ___ the minister's gaffe to demand his resignation.

questions.explanation: 'Drive at' means to try to express or suggest: What exactly are you driving at?

wrongReasons.to: 'drive to' refers to travelling to a place, not to an intended meaning.
wrongReasons.for: 'drive for' is not used with this meaning.

questions.text: I'm not sure what she's driving ___, but I suspect she wants a pay rise.

questions.explanation: 'Tail off' means to gradually decrease: Interest tailed off after the first week.

wrongReasons.down: 'tail down' is not a phrasal verb in English.
wrongReasons.out: 'tail out' does not exist; decline is expressed by 'tail off'.

questions.text: Sales have tailed ___ sharply since a cheaper competitor arrived.

questions.explanation: 'Back down (on something)' means to withdraw a demand or position: The council backed down on the plan.

wrongReasons.up: 'back up' means to support someone, the opposite idea.
wrongReasons.out: 'back out' means to withdraw from an agreement already made, and is followed by 'of', not 'on'.

questions.text: The striking workers refused to back ___ on their demands despite threats of dismissal.

questions.explanation: 'Wear off' means to gradually disappear: The effects of the painkiller wore off.

wrongReasons.out: 'wear out' means to become unusable through use, or to exhaust someone.
wrongReasons.away: 'wear away' means physical erosion, as with rocks or steps.

questions.text: The novelty of living in the countryside soon wore ___.

questions.explanation: 'Reel off' means to say a list quickly and easily: He reeled off the names of every player.

wrongReasons.out: 'reel out' is used for unwinding a line or cable, not for reciting.
wrongReasons.up: 'reel up' does not mean to recite; the phrasal verb is 'reel off'.

questions.text: She reeled ___ a long list of complaints without pausing for breath.

questions.explanation: 'Fall through' means to fail to happen: Our holiday plans fell through.

wrongReasons.down: 'fall down' is used for physical falling or for an argument being weak.
wrongReasons.out: 'fall out' means to argue and stop being friendly.

questions.text: The sale of the house fell ___ at the last minute when the buyer's mortgage was refused.

questions.explanation: 'Face up to' means to accept and deal with something difficult: She faced up to her fears.

wrongReasons.on: 'face on to' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.with: 'face with' is used in the passive (faced with a problem), not before 'to'.

questions.text: It's high time you faced ___ to the consequences of your actions.

questions.explanation: 'Lay off' means to dismiss workers, usually because there is not enough work.

wrongReasons.down: 'lay down' means to establish rules or put something down.
wrongReasons.out: 'lay out' means to arrange or to spend money.

questions.text: The struggling airline was forced to lay ___ a third of its workforce.

questions.explanation: 'Talk your way out of something' means to escape a situation by clever talking.

wrongReasons.off: 'talk off' is not used with 'of' in this meaning.
wrongReasons.away: 'talk away' means to talk continuously; it does not take 'of something'.

questions.text: He was so charming that he could talk his way ___ of almost any difficulty.

questions.explanation: 'Sift through' means to examine a large amount of material carefully.

wrongReasons.into: 'sift into' does not express careful searching.
wrongReasons.over: 'sift over' is not the standard phrasal verb; use 'sift through'.

questions.text: Rescue workers are still sifting ___ the rubble for survivors.

questions.explanation: 'Peter out' means to gradually come to an end: The path petered out in the woods.

wrongReasons.away: 'peter away' is not English; the phrasal verb is 'peter out'.

questions.text: The protest petered ___ once the rain started.

questions.explanation: 'Come out' means to become known: The full story came out at the trial.

wrongReasons.up: 'come up' means to be mentioned or to arise, not to be revealed.
wrongReasons.off: 'come off' means to succeed or to become detached.

questions.text: I wouldn't want to be in her shoes when the truth comes ___.

questions.explanation: 'Branch out (into)' means to start doing something new: The bakery branched out into catering.

wrongReasons.off: 'branch off' means to leave a main road or topic.
wrongReasons.away: 'branch away' is not a phrasal verb.

questions.text: The company has branched ___ into renewable energy over the last decade.

questions.explanation: 'Egg someone on' means to encourage them to do something foolish or risky.

wrongReasons.out: 'egg out' does not exist; the phrasal verb is 'egg on'.

questions.text: The teenagers were egging each other ___ to jump off the harbour wall.

questions.explanation: 'Dream up' means to invent a plan or idea, often an unusual one.

wrongReasons.out: 'dream out' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.off: 'dream off' does not exist; inventing a plan is 'dream up'.

questions.text: The scheme was dreamt ___ over a few drinks and was never properly costed.

questions.explanation: 'Pull out (of)' means to withdraw from an event or agreement.

wrongReasons.off: 'pull off' means to succeed in something difficult.
wrongReasons.away: 'pull away' means to move ahead or move away; it does not take 'of the tournament'.

questions.text: The champion had to pull ___ of the tournament with a wrist injury.

questions.explanation: 'Weed out' means to remove unwanted elements from a group.

wrongReasons.away: 'weed away' is not a phrasal verb; removing unwanted items is 'weed out'.

questions.text: The new manager quickly weeded ___ the least productive projects.

questions.explanation: 'Let up' means to become less strong or stop: The wind showed no sign of letting up.

wrongReasons.off: 'let off' means to excuse from punishment or to fire a gun or firework.

questions.text: The rain has finally let ___, so we can set off now.

questions.explanation: 'Palm someone off with something' means to trick them into accepting something inferior.

wrongReasons.out: 'palm out' is not a phrasal verb.

questions.text: The tourists were palmed ___ with cheap imitations instead of genuine antiques.

questions.explanation: 'Drown out' means to make a sound impossible to hear with a louder noise.

wrongReasons.down: 'drown down' is not English; a louder noise drowns something out.

questions.text: The speaker was drowned ___ by heckling from the back of the hall.

questions.explanation: 'Brush up (on)' means to improve a skill you have partly forgotten.

wrongReasons.on: 'brush on on' repeats the preposition; the phrasal verb is 'brush up on'.
wrongReasons.off: 'brush off' means to ignore or dismiss someone.

questions.text: I really need to brush ___ on my Portuguese before the conference in Lisbon.

questions.explanation: 'Laugh something off' means to treat a problem as unimportant by joking about it.

wrongReasons.out: 'laugh out' is used in 'laugh out loud' and cannot take an object like 'the allegations'.
wrongReasons.away: 'laugh away' means to laugh continuously; it does not mean to dismiss.

questions.text: The minister tried to laugh ___ the allegations, but the evidence was overwhelming.

questions.explanation: Formal letters often open with 'with regard to' or 'in regard to' (= about): I am writing with regard to your invoice.

wrongReasons.on: The fixed formal phrase is 'with regard to', not 'on regard to'.
wrongReasons.about: 'about regard to' is ungrammatical; 'about' alone would replace the whole phrase.

questions.text: I am writing ___ regard to your letter of 12 March concerning the delayed shipment.

questions.explanation: 'Do not hesitate to contact me' is a standard formal closing in business letters.

wrongReasons.call up: 'call up' is informal and needs an object between the parts (call me up); the formal verb is 'contact'.
wrongReasons.ask: 'ask me' does not fit 'should you require information'; the formula is 'do not hesitate to contact me'.

questions.text: Please do not hesitate to ___ me should you require any further information.

questions.explanation: Formal notices use verbs like 'be reminded / advised / informed that': Customers are advised that the store closes at six.

wrongReasons.said: 'said' cannot take a person as its object in the passive (Passengers are said that...); use 'reminded' or 'informed'.
wrongReasons.explained: 'explain' does not take a person as a direct object, so 'Passengers are explained that' is wrong.

questions.text: Passengers are ___ that smoking is prohibited throughout the terminal building.

questions.explanation: In British formal letters, 'Dear Sir or Madam' is closed with 'Yours faithfully'; 'Dear Ms Lee' is closed with 'Yours sincerely'.

wrongReasons.sincerely: 'Yours sincerely' is used when you address the reader by name, not after 'Dear Sir or Madam'.
wrongReasons.truly: 'Yours truly' is mainly American and less formal; British convention requires 'Yours faithfully'.

questions.text: Her letter began 'Dear Sir or Madam', so she correctly ended it 'Yours ___'.

questions.explanation: 'Refrain from + -ing' is a formal way to ask people not to do something: Please refrain from smoking.

wrongReasons.avoid: 'avoid' takes the -ing form directly, without 'from': 'avoid using', not 'avoid from using'.
wrongReasons.stop: 'stop from using' needs an object (stop someone from); the formal verb before 'from' is 'refrain'.

questions.text: Readers are kindly requested to ___ from using mobile phones in the reading room.

questions.explanation: 'No later than' + date sets a formal deadline: Applications must arrive no later than Friday.

wrongReasons.then: 'then' is about time sequence; the comparative structure needs 'than'.
wrongReasons.to: 'later to' is ungrammatical; comparatives are followed by 'than'.

questions.text: Payment must be received no later ___ 30 June, or the booking will be cancelled.

questions.explanation: 'I should / would be grateful if you could...' is a polite formal request.

wrongReasons.that: 'grateful that' expresses thanks for a fact, not a request; for a request use 'if you could'.
wrongReasons.for: 'grateful for' is followed by a noun or -ing form, not by 'you could'.

questions.text: I should be grateful ___ you could send me a copy of the minutes.

questions.explanation: In formal relative clauses, 'of which' follows the noun: the contents of which...

wrongReasons.that: 'that' cannot follow a preposition; after 'of' we need 'which'.
wrongReasons.it: 'of it' would create a comma splice; a relative pronoun ('which') is needed.

questions.text: Thank you for your letter of 3 May, the contents of ___ have been carefully noted.

questions.explanation: Informal 'Fancy + -ing?' is a casual invitation: Fancy grabbing a coffee?

wrongReasons.to go: 'Fancy' is followed by the -ing form, not a to-infinitive.
wrongReasons.go: After 'Fancy' we need the -ing form: 'Fancy going?'

questions.text: Fancy ___ for a quick drink after work tonight?

questions.explanation: Hotel notices use formal passive verbs such as 'Guests are requested to...'.

wrongReasons.please: 'are please to' is ungrammatical; the polite formal verb is 'requested'.
wrongReasons.wanted: 'are wanted to' is not English; formal notices say 'are requested to'.

questions.text: Guests are ___ to vacate their rooms by 11 a.m. on the day of departure.

questions.explanation: 'We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause' is a fixed formal apology.

wrongReasons.do: 'do inconvenience' is not a collocation; use 'cause'.

questions.text: We apologise for any inconvenience this may ___.

questions.explanation: Formal instructions often use 'notify / inform us in writing'.

wrongReasons.say: 'say' does not take a person as a direct object; you 'tell' or 'notify' someone.
wrongReasons.speak: 'speak us' is ungrammatical; it would need 'to', and it contradicts 'in writing'.

questions.text: Should you wish to cancel your subscription, please ___ us in writing.

questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form: I look forward to meeting you.

wrongReasons.hear: 'to' here is a preposition, so the verb must be 'hearing', not the base form.
wrongReasons.heard: A past participle cannot follow the preposition 'to'; use 'hearing'.

questions.text: I look forward to ___ from you at your earliest convenience.

questions.explanation: 'Free of charge' is the formal fixed phrase for 'free'.

wrongReasons.cost: The fixed phrase is 'free of charge', not 'free of cost'.
wrongReasons.pay: 'pay' is a verb here; the noun in the phrase is 'charge'.

questions.text: Admission to the exhibition is free of ___ for children under twelve.

questions.explanation: 'Owing to' (= because of) is a formal linker followed by a noun: Owing to illness, she resigned.

wrongReasons.for: 'owing for' means owing money for something; the linker is 'owing to'.
wrongReasons.of: 'owing of' is not English; use 'owing to'.

questions.text: Owing ___ unforeseen circumstances, tonight's performance has been cancelled.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': The account will be closed unless you pay.

wrongReasons.if: 'if payment is received' reverses the meaning: the account would be suspended because you paid.
wrongReasons.except: 'except' is not a conjunction before a full clause here; use 'unless'.

questions.text: Your account will be suspended ___ payment is received within seven days.

questions.explanation: 'Prior to' is a formal equivalent of 'before' and is followed by a noun or -ing form.

wrongReasons.of: The formal phrase is 'prior to', not 'prior of'.
wrongReasons.from: 'prior from' is not English; use 'prior to'.

questions.text: Prior ___ commencing the work, the contractor must obtain a building permit.

questions.explanation: 'In the event of' + noun is a formal way to say 'if there is': In the event of an emergency, call 999.

wrongReasons.that: 'in the event that' must be followed by a full clause (that a fire breaks out), not just a noun.
wrongReasons.for: The fixed phrase is 'in the event of', not 'for'.

questions.text: In the event ___ fire, do not use the lifts.

questions.explanation: Informal British English uses 'give someone a ring / bell / buzz' for phoning them.

wrongReasons.phone: 'phone' is a verb or a device; you 'give someone a ring' or 'a call', not 'a phone'.
wrongReasons.telephone: 'give me a telephone' is wrong and too formal; use 'a ring' or 'a call'.

questions.text: Give me a ___ when you get to the station and I'll come and pick you up.

questions.explanation: Formal notices say 'accepts no responsibility / liability for'.

wrongReasons.blame: 'accept no blame' is used for faults in the past, not as a formal disclaimer.
wrongReasons.fault: 'accept no fault' is not the formal collocation; use 'responsibility'.

questions.text: The management accepts no ___ for items left unattended in the changing rooms.

questions.explanation: 'Should any problems arise' is a formal conditional with inversion (= if any problems arise).

wrongReasons.raise: 'raise' is transitive and needs an object (raise a question); problems 'arise'.
wrongReasons.rise: 'rise' means to go up; problems 'arise', they do not 'rise'.

questions.text: Should any problems ___, please contact the helpdesk immediately.

questions.explanation: 'Pursuant to' (= in accordance with) is a legal formal phrase.

wrongReasons.with: The legal phrase is 'pursuant to', not 'pursuant with'.
wrongReasons.of: 'pursuant of' is not used; say 'pursuant to'.

questions.text: Pursuant ___ clause 4 of the agreement, the tenant shall maintain the garden.

questions.explanation: Formal notices use passive verbs such as 'will not be considered'.

wrongReasons.looked: 'looked' needs 'at' (looked at); on its own it does not fit.
wrongReasons.thought: 'thought' needs 'about' and is too informal here; use 'considered'.

questions.text: Applications received after the closing date will not be ___.

questions.explanation: Formal announcements use the passive 'are taken with you'.

wrongReasons.take: After 'are' the passive needs the past participle 'taken'.
wrongReasons.took: 'took' is the past simple; the passive needs the participle 'taken'.

questions.text: Kindly ensure that all personal belongings are ___ with you when leaving the train.

questions.explanation: 'We would appreciate it if you could...' is a polite formal request; 'it' is required.

wrongReasons.like: 'would like it if' is possible but informal; the standard formal formula is 'would appreciate it'.
wrongReasons.thank: 'thank it' makes no sense; you thank a person, not 'it'.

questions.text: We would ___ it if you could reply by Friday.

questions.explanation: 'Long time no see' is a fixed informal greeting, used exactly in this form.

wrongReasons.seen: The informal expression is fixed: 'long time no see', not 'seen'.
wrongReasons.saw: 'saw' is not used; the expression is 'long time no see'.

questions.text: Hey, long time no ___! How've you been?

questions.explanation: 'On behalf of' means 'representing': She spoke on behalf of her colleagues.

wrongReasons.part: 'on part of' is wrong; 'on the part of' means 'by', not 'representing'.
wrongReasons.half: 'on half of' is not English; the formal phrase is 'on behalf of'.

questions.text: I'd like to thank you on ___ of the whole team for your generous support.

questions.explanation: 'In the strictest confidence' is a formal fixed expression meaning 'completely secretly'.

wrongReasons.confidential: 'confidential' is an adjective; after 'the strictest' we need the noun 'confidence'.
wrongReasons.secret: 'in the strictest secret' is not the fixed phrase; use 'confidence'.

questions.text: The information you provide will be treated in the strictest ___.

questions.explanation: Formal instructions say queries should be 'directed / addressed to' a department.

wrongReasons.asked: You ask a question, but queries are not 'asked to' a department; use 'directed to'.
wrongReasons.said: 'said to' does not fit; queries are 'addressed to' someone.

questions.text: All queries should be ___ to the Human Resources department.

questions.explanation: 'It has come to our attention that' is a formal way to say 'we have noticed'.

wrongReasons.mind: 'come to our mind' means to be remembered or thought of, not to be noticed officially.
wrongReasons.eyes: 'come to our eyes' is not an English expression.

questions.text: It has come to our ___ that several invoices remain unpaid.

questions.explanation: Legal forms use 'hereby' + a performative verb: I hereby declare that...

wrongReasons.says: 'says' is too informal for a legal declaration; use 'declares' or 'certifies'.
wrongReasons.tells: 'tell' needs a person as object (tells you that); a formal declaration uses 'declares'.

questions.text: The undersigned hereby ___ that the information given above is true and complete.

questions.explanation: Organisations 'issue' or 'offer' an apology in formal statements.

wrongReasons.said: You 'say sorry', but you do not 'say an apology'.
wrongReasons.told: 'tell an apology' is not a collocation; companies 'issue' one.

questions.text: The company has formally ___ an apology for the distress caused to its customers.

questions.explanation: After 'under no circumstances' at the start of a clause, formal English inverts subject and auxiliary: Under no circumstances will we accept cash.

wrongReasons.are: 'are refunds be given' has two verbs; inversion needs a modal: 'will refunds be given'.
wrongReasons.do: 'do refunds be given' is ungrammatical; 'be' needs a modal, not 'do'.

questions.text: Tickets may be exchanged, but under no circumstances ___ refunds be given.

questions.explanation: Register contrasts informal (chatty) and formal (professional) tone: A report needs a formal tone.

wrongReasons.chattier: The contrast with 'chatty' requires the opposite register, not more of the same.
wrongReasons.casual: 'casual' is informal, so it does not contrast with 'chatty'.

questions.text: Whereas the first draft was rather chatty, the final version adopts a more ___ tone suitable for the board.

questions.explanation: After expressions like 'it is essential / vital / imperative that', formal English uses the base form (or 'should' + base form): It is vital that he be told.

wrongReasons.is: After 'it is essential that' formal English uses the subjunctive 'be', not the indicative 'is'.
wrongReasons.are: 'every passenger' is singular, and the subjunctive form is always 'be'.

questions.text: It is essential that every passenger ___ in possession of a valid ticket before boarding.

questions.explanation: After 'demand that', use the subjunctive base form for every person: They demanded that she be dismissed.

wrongReasons.is: 'demanded' is past, and the formal subjunctive is 'be', so 'is' is doubly wrong.
wrongReasons.to be: 'demand that' introduces a clause with a subject and a base-form verb, not a to-infinitive.

questions.text: The shareholders demanded that the chief executive ___ present at the emergency hearing.

questions.explanation: Unreal present conditionals use 'were' for all persons (informally 'was'): If I were rich, I'd travel.

wrongReasons.am: 'If I am you' is impossible; the situation is unreal, so use 'were'.
wrongReasons.be: 'If I be you' is not used in modern English; the form is 'If I were you'.

questions.text: If I ___ you, I would accept the offer without a moment's hesitation.

questions.explanation: 'Wish' + past perfect expresses regret about the past: I wish I had studied harder.

wrongReasons.have: 'I wish I have listened' is wrong; regret about the past needs the past perfect 'had listened'.
wrongReasons.would: 'I wish I would' is not used about your own past actions; use 'had listened'.

questions.text: I wish I ___ listened to my grandfather's advice when I was younger.

questions.explanation: 'It's (high) time' + subject + past simple means something should already have happened: It's time we left.

wrongReasons.takes: 'It's high time' is followed by a past form, not the present 'takes'.
wrongReasons.take: The base form is wrong here; 'It's high time' needs the past simple 'took'.

questions.text: It's high time the council ___ action on the derelict buildings in the centre.

questions.explanation: 'As though / as if' + past form shows an unreal comparison: She acts as if she were the boss.

wrongReasons.is: 'is' suggests he really is the owner, but the sentence says he is not; use 'were'.
wrongReasons.be: 'as though he be' is not modern English; use 'were'.

questions.text: He talks as though he ___ the owner of the company, but he's only a junior clerk.

questions.explanation: 'Far be it from me to...' is a fixed subjunctive expression used before a criticism.

wrongReasons.is: The fixed expression uses the subjunctive: 'Far be it from me', not 'Far is it'.
wrongReasons.was: 'Far was it from me' is not the idiom; it is always 'Far be it from me'.

questions.text: Far ___ it from me to criticise, but your report is rather long.

questions.explanation: 'Come what may' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'whatever happens'.

wrongReasons.might: The fixed expression is 'come what may', not 'might'.
wrongReasons.will: 'come what will' is not the idiom; it is 'come what may'.

questions.text: Come what ___, we will finish the bridge before the rainy season.

questions.explanation: 'Suffice it to say that...' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'I will only say that'.

wrongReasons.said: After 'to' we need the base form: 'Suffice it to say'.
wrongReasons.tell: The fixed expression is 'suffice it to say'; 'tell' would need a listener as object.

questions.text: Suffice it to ___ that the evening did not go entirely as planned.

questions.explanation: After 'order that', formal English uses the subjunctive: The court ordered that the land be returned.

wrongReasons.is: 'ordered that ... is' uses the indicative; formal English requires the subjunctive 'be'.
wrongReasons.was: After 'order that', even in the past, the subjunctive 'be' is used, not 'was'.

questions.text: The judge ordered that the defendant ___ held in custody until the trial.

questions.explanation: 'Would that' (literary) means 'I wish' and is followed by a past form for present wishes.

wrongReasons.have: 'Would that' expresses an unreal wish, so we need the past form 'had'.
wrongReasons.would have: 'Would that I would have' doubles the modal; the pattern is 'Would that I had'.

questions.text: Would that I ___ the courage to tell her how I really feel!

questions.explanation: 'Be that as it may' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'despite that'.

wrongReasons.might: The idiom is fixed: 'Be that as it may', never 'might'.
wrongReasons.is: 'Be that as it is' is not the idiom; use 'may'.

questions.text: Be that as it ___, we still need a decision by Monday.

questions.explanation: 'Would rather' + another subject + past simple expresses a preference about the present or future: I'd rather you stayed.

wrongReasons.don't: After 'I'd rather you', use a past form: 'didn't tell', not 'don't tell'.
wrongReasons.won't: 'I'd rather you won't' is wrong; the structure takes the past simple 'didn't'.

questions.text: I'd rather you ___ tell anyone about the merger just yet.

questions.explanation: In a negative subjunctive, 'not' comes before the base form: It is vital that he not be moved.

wrongReasons.is: After 'it is vital that', formal English uses the base form 'be', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.will be: 'will be' is not used after 'it is vital that'; use 'be' or 'should be'.

questions.text: It is vital that the patient ___ not disturbed during the night.

questions.explanation: Inverted conditional 'Were + subject + to + infinitive' = 'If the company were to collapse'.

wrongReasons.going: 'Were the company going collapse' is ungrammatical; the inverted form is 'Were ... to collapse'.
wrongReasons.will: A modal cannot follow 'Were the company'; use 'to'.

questions.text: Were the company ___ collapse, thousands of jobs would be lost.

questions.explanation: 'Had it not been for' = 'If it had not been for' (third conditional, inverted).

wrongReasons.was: 'Had it not was' combines two auxiliaries; the form is 'had it not been'.

questions.text: Had it not ___ for the lifeguard, the boy would have drowned.

questions.explanation: 'Supposing' + 'were to' (or 'should') introduces an unlikely hypothetical situation: Supposing she were to leave, who would replace her?

wrongReasons.would: 'would' belongs in the main clause (what would we do), not after 'Supposing'; use 'were to refuse'.
wrongReasons.will: 'Supposing he will refuse' is too real for this hypothetical; use 'were to' or 'should'.

questions.text: Supposing he ___ refuse, what would we do then?

questions.explanation: 'If only' + past perfect expresses strong regret about the past.

wrongReasons.have: 'If only I have known' is wrong; regret about the past takes the past perfect.
wrongReasons.would have: 'If only I would have known' is not standard English; use 'had known'.

questions.text: If only I ___ known how expensive the repairs would be!

questions.explanation: 'Heaven forbid (that)...' is a fixed subjunctive phrase expressing a strong wish that something won't happen.

wrongReasons.forbids: The subjunctive has no -s ending: 'Heaven forbid'.
wrongReasons.forbade: The expression is fixed in the present subjunctive: 'Heaven forbid'.

questions.text: Heaven ___ that anyone should find out about this!

questions.explanation: After expressions like 'it is essential / vital / imperative that', formal English uses the base form (or 'should' + base form): It is vital that he be told.

wrongReasons.are: In formal English, 'it is imperative that' takes the subjunctive 'be', not 'are'.
wrongReasons.were: 'were' is used for unreal situations; after 'imperative that' use 'be'.

questions.text: It is imperative that all documents ___ signed before noon tomorrow.

questions.explanation: 'Would sooner' + another subject + past simple expresses preference, like 'would rather'.

wrongReasons.keep: After 'I'd sooner you', the verb is in the past: 'kept'.
wrongReasons.will keep: 'I'd sooner you will keep' is ungrammatical; use the past simple.

questions.text: I'd sooner you ___ your opinions to yourself in future.

questions.explanation: After 'whether', very formal English may use the subjunctive 'be'; 'is' is the normal neutral form.

wrongReasons.being: A clause after 'whether' needs a finite verb, not 'being'.

questions.text: Whether he ___ guilty or innocent, he deserves a fair trial.

questions.explanation: 'It's about time' + subject + past simple criticises a delay: It's about time you found a job.

wrongReasons.go: After 'It's about time you', the verb must be in the past: 'went'.
wrongReasons.will go: 'It's about time you will go' is ungrammatical; use 'went'.

questions.text: It's about time you ___ to bed; it's well past midnight.

questions.explanation: 'As if' + past perfect describes an unreal situation before the time of the main verb.

wrongReasons.has: The main verb 'strolled' is past, so we need the past perfect 'had happened'.
wrongReasons.would: 'as if nothing would happened' is ungrammatical; use 'had happened'.

questions.text: He strolled into the meeting as if nothing ___ happened.

questions.explanation: 'Lest' (= so that not) is followed by the subjunctive or 'should' + base form.

wrongReasons.is: After 'lest', formal English uses the subjunctive 'be', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.will be: 'lest anyone will be' is not used; use 'be' or 'should be'.

questions.text: Lest anyone ___ in any doubt, I have no intention of resigning.

questions.explanation: 'If + were to' describes an unlikely future event: If you were to win, what would you do?

wrongReasons.is: 'If it is to rain' does not match 'would move'; use 'were to'.

questions.text: If it ___ to rain on the day, the ceremony would move indoors.

questions.explanation: 'Wish + would' expresses annoyance and a desire for someone else's behaviour to change.

wrongReasons.should: 'I wish they should stop' is not used; the pattern is 'wish + would'.

questions.text: I wish the neighbours ___ stop playing loud music after midnight.

questions.explanation: After 'it is recommended that', formal English uses 'be' or 'should be' + past participle.

wrongReasons.is: The formal subjunctive is 'be', not the indicative 'is'.
wrongReasons.being: 'being' is not a finite verb; the clause needs 'be'.

questions.text: It is recommended that the medicine ___ taken with food.

questions.explanation: The subjunctive 'be' is used for all persons after 'it is crucial that'.

wrongReasons.is: After 'it is crucial that', use the subjunctive 'be'.
wrongReasons.was: Past forms are not used here; the subjunctive is 'be'.

questions.text: It is crucial that the minister ___ informed of the changes as soon as possible.

questions.explanation: 'Woe betide...' is a fixed subjunctive phrase warning that someone will be in trouble.

wrongReasons.betides: The subjunctive has no -s ending: 'Woe betide'.
wrongReasons.beside: 'beside' is a preposition; the idiom is 'woe betide'.

questions.text: Woe ___ anyone who forgets her birthday this year!

questions.explanation: 'As it were' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'so to speak'.

wrongReasons.was: The idiom is fixed: 'as it were', never 'as it was'.
wrongReasons.is: 'as it is' means 'in the present situation', a different idiom.

questions.text: He is, as it ___, the architect of his own misfortune.

questions.explanation: 'Long live...' is a fixed subjunctive wish: Long live the king!

wrongReasons.lives: The subjunctive has no -s: 'Long live', not 'lives'.
wrongReasons.living: 'Long living' is not English; the formula is 'Long live'.

questions.text: Long ___ the free press!

questions.explanation: After 'stipulate that', formal English uses the subjunctive base form.

wrongReasons.is: 'stipulate that' takes the subjunctive 'be', not 'is'.
wrongReasons.must to be: 'must to be' is ungrammatical; modals are followed by the base form without 'to'.

questions.text: The regulations stipulate that each candidate ___ present in person to sit the examination.

questions.explanation: 'So be it' is a fixed subjunctive phrase meaning 'I accept that'.

wrongReasons.is: The idiom uses the subjunctive: 'So be it', not 'So is it'.
wrongReasons.let: 'So let it' is incomplete; the idiom is 'So be it'.

questions.text: So ___ it: if the committee refuses, we will appeal.

questions.explanation: 'Circumstantial evidence' suggests guilt indirectly, without direct proof: The case rested on circumstantial evidence.

wrongReasons.circumstance: 'circumstance' is a noun; before 'evidence' we need the adjective 'circumstantial'.
wrongReasons.incidental: 'incidental' means minor or accidental; it is not the legal term for indirect evidence.

questions.text: The evidence against him was purely ___; nobody had actually seen him at the scene.

questions.explanation: 'A renaissance / revival' is a period of new life after decline: Jazz is enjoying a revival.

wrongReasons.revive: 'revive' is a verb; after 'a' we need a noun such as 'revival'.
wrongReasons.survival: 'survival' means continuing to exist, not returning to life after decline.

questions.text: After decades of decline, the old port is enjoying something of a ___, with galleries and cafés opening every month.

questions.explanation: 'A qualified success' is a success with some reservations: The tour was a qualified success.

wrongReasons.total: 'a total success' contradicts the problem mentioned after 'but'.
wrongReasons.complete: 'complete' denies the reservations that the second half of the sentence describes.

questions.text: The new law has been a ___ success: crime has fallen, but the prisons are overcrowded.

questions.explanation: 'A penchant / propensity for' means a natural tendency to do something.

wrongReasons.tend: 'tend' is a verb; after 'a' we need a noun such as 'tendency'.

questions.text: He has a ___ for exaggeration, so take his stories with a pinch of salt.

questions.explanation: 'Send shockwaves through' means to cause shock and disturbance: The news sent shockwaves through the industry.

wrongReasons.shocks: The collocation is 'send shockwaves through', not 'send shocks through'.
wrongReasons.waves: 'waves' alone does not convey shock; the fixed phrase is 'shockwaves'.

questions.text: The chief executive's sudden resignation sent ___ through the financial markets.

questions.explanation: 'A white elephant' is an expensive possession or project that is useless.

wrongReasons.whale: The idiom is 'white elephant', not 'white whale'.
wrongReasons.horse: 'white horse' has no idiomatic meaning of a useless project.

questions.text: The project turned out to be a complete white ___, costing millions and benefiting nobody.

questions.explanation: 'The crux / heart of the matter' is the most important point.

wrongReasons.centre: 'the centre of the matter' is not idiomatic; use 'the crux' or 'the heart'.
wrongReasons.middle: 'the middle of the matter' is not English; use 'the heart of the matter'.

questions.text: The ___ of the matter is that we simply cannot afford a second runway.

questions.explanation: 'Hit an all-time low/high' means to reach the lowest/highest level ever.

wrongReasons.lowest: The fixed phrase uses the noun 'low': 'an all-time low'.
wrongReasons.bottom: 'an all-time bottom' is not idiomatic; use 'an all-time low'.

questions.text: Following the scandal, the prime minister's approval ratings hit an all-time ___.

questions.explanation: 'On the verge / brink of' means very close to something, usually bad.

wrongReasons.border: 'on the border of' refers to geographical borders, not to being close to disaster.
wrongReasons.limit: 'on the limit of' is not idiomatic; use 'on the brink of'.

questions.text: The family business is teetering on the ___ of bankruptcy.

questions.explanation: 'Set a precedent' means to establish an example to be followed later.

wrongReasons.president: 'president' is a head of state; the legal word is 'precedent'.
wrongReasons.precedence: 'precedence' means priority (take precedence); you 'set a precedent'.

questions.text: The Supreme Court's ruling set a ___ for future cases of this kind.

questions.explanation: 'Like chalk and cheese' (British) describes two people who are completely different.

wrongReasons.bread: 'bread and cheese' go together; the idiom for opposites is 'chalk and cheese'.
wrongReasons.wine: 'wine and cheese' is a pairing, not an idiom for opposites.

questions.text: The two brothers are like ___ and cheese; they have nothing whatsoever in common.

questions.explanation: 'Out of hand' (= immediately, without consideration) is used with 'reject / dismiss'.

wrongReasons.mind: 'out of mind' (as in 'out of sight, out of mind') does not mean immediately.
wrongReasons.order: 'out of order' means broken or unacceptable, not 'without consideration'.

questions.text: The proposal was dismissed out of ___ without any serious discussion.

questions.explanation: 'On the edge of your seat' means very excited or nervous to know what happens.

wrongReasons.side: The idiom is 'on the edge of their seats', not 'side'.
wrongReasons.border: 'border' is not used in this idiom.

questions.text: The film's final twist kept the audience on the ___ of their seats.

questions.explanation: 'Like gold dust' (British) means very rare and in high demand.

wrongReasons.bars: The idiom is 'like gold dust', not 'gold bars'.
wrongReasons.coins: 'gold coins' is literal and not part of the idiom.

questions.text: Tickets for the final were like gold ___; they sold out within minutes.

questions.explanation: 'Take something at face value' means to accept it as it appears, without questioning.

wrongReasons.price: The idiom is 'face value', not 'face price'.

questions.text: Don't take his promises at face ___; he has broken every one so far.

questions.explanation: 'A clean bill of health' means official confirmation that something is in good condition.

wrongReasons.money: The idiom is 'a clean bill of health', not 'money'.
wrongReasons.sale: 'bill of sale' is a legal document of purchase, a different expression.

questions.text: After a thorough inspection, the auditors gave the charity a clean bill of ___.

questions.explanation: 'Behind closed doors' means privately, without the public being informed.

wrongReasons.curtains: The idiom is 'behind closed doors', not 'curtains'.

questions.text: The decision was taken behind closed ___, without consulting the staff.

questions.explanation: 'A foregone conclusion' is a result that is certain before it happens.

wrongReasons.result: The fixed phrase is 'foregone conclusion', not 'foregone result'.

questions.text: With the opposition in disarray, the election result was a foregone ___.

questions.explanation: 'Financially viable' means able to succeed without losing money.

wrongReasons.available: 'available' means ready to use; it does not describe whether a plan can make money.
wrongReasons.valuable: 'valuable' means worth a lot; 'viable' means able to work.

questions.text: The scheme was abandoned because it was not financially ___.

questions.explanation: 'Take something in your stride' means to deal with a problem calmly.

wrongReasons.step: The idiom is 'in your stride', not 'in your step'.

questions.text: Despite the harsh reviews, she took the criticism in her ___ and started on her next novel.

questions.explanation: 'In its infancy' means at a very early stage of development.

wrongReasons.childhood: For projects we say 'in its infancy', not 'childhood'.
wrongReasons.birth: 'in its birth' is not idiomatic; use 'in its infancy'.

questions.text: The research programme is still in its ___, so it is too early to judge its impact.

questions.explanation: 'At a delicate juncture / stage' means at a sensitive moment in a process.

wrongReasons.step: 'at a delicate step' is not idiomatic; use 'stage' or 'juncture'.
wrongReasons.place: 'place' refers to location, not a moment in a process.

questions.text: The peace talks are at a delicate ___, so the envoy declined to comment.

questions.explanation: 'On the back burner' means postponed or given low priority.

wrongReasons.seat: 'take a back seat' is a different idiom meaning to have a less active role.
wrongReasons.shelf: The idiom is 'on the back burner'; 'on the shelf' is a separate expression.

questions.text: Plans for the new stadium have been put on the back ___ until the economy recovers.

questions.explanation: 'Be acquitted / cleared of' means to be declared not guilty.

wrongReasons.acquired: 'acquired' means obtained; the legal term is 'acquitted'.
wrongReasons.released: 'released' takes 'from', not 'of'; 'acquitted of' is the legal collocation.

questions.text: After a two-week trial, she was ___ of all charges and walked free from court.

questions.explanation: 'Nothing short of' + adjective/noun means 'really, truly': It was nothing short of a disaster.

wrongReasons.to: The fixed phrase is 'nothing short of', not 'short to'.
wrongReasons.from: 'short from' is not used in this expression.

questions.text: Her recovery after the accident was nothing short ___ miraculous.

questions.explanation: 'A U-turn' is a complete change of policy.

wrongReasons.back: 'U-back' is not a word; the expression is 'U-turn'.

questions.text: Under pressure from voters, the government made a humiliating U-___ on tuition fees.

questions.explanation: 'Come under fire / attack' means to be strongly criticised.

wrongReasons.critique: The collocation is 'come under criticism' or 'fire'; 'come under critique' is not idiomatic.
wrongReasons.shoot: 'shoot' is a verb; the idiom uses the noun 'fire'.

questions.text: The ministry's handling of the floods came under ___ from all sides.

questions.explanation: 'Under the weather' means slightly ill.

wrongReasons.cloud: 'under a cloud' means in disgrace, a different idiom.
wrongReasons.rain: 'under the rain' is not idiomatic for feeling ill.

questions.text: I've been feeling a bit under the ___ all week, so I'm staying in tonight.

questions.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' means to end a quarrel and become friends.

wrongReasons.axe: The idiom is fixed: 'bury the hatchet', not 'axe'.

questions.text: After years of rivalry, the two founders finally agreed to bury the ___.

questions.explanation: 'Open to interpretation' means able to be understood in different ways.

wrongReasons.possible: 'possible to interpretations' is ungrammatical; use 'open to'.
wrongReasons.available: 'available to' means accessible to people, not capable of being interpreted.

questions.text: The survey data are ___ to several different interpretations.

questions.explanation: 'A bolt from the blue' is a complete surprise.

wrongReasons.sky: The idiom is 'a bolt from the blue', not 'from the sky'.
wrongReasons.sun: 'from the sun' is not part of the idiom.

questions.text: Her decision to emigrate came as a bolt from the ___ to her family.

questions.explanation: 'Irrelevant / immaterial to' means not connected with the matter being considered.

wrongReasons.irrelevance: 'irrelevance' is a noun; after 'deemed' we need an adjective.
wrongReasons.relevant: 'relevant' contradicts the fact that the testimony was disregarded.

questions.text: The witness's testimony was deemed ___ to the case and was disregarded by the jury.

questions.explanation: 'Root out' means to find and completely remove something bad.

wrongReasons.up: 'root up' means to dig up a plant; for corruption we say 'root out'.
wrongReasons.off: 'root off' is not a phrasal verb.

questions.text: The new chairman has pledged to root ___ corruption at every level of the organisation.

questions.explanation: 'Allay fears' means to make people less worried.

wrongReasons.alloy: 'alloy' is a mixture of metals; the verb is 'allay'.
wrongReasons.relieve of: 'relieve of' needs a person as object (relieve someone of a burden); it does not fit 'fears'.

questions.text: The minister's evasive answers did little to ___ the public's fears.
